paragraflar: CASE OF ÖZAKÇA AND GÜLMEN v. TÜRKİYE
(Applications nos. 45940/17 and 46171/17)

Art 2 and Art 3 (substantive) • Positive obligations • Adequate medical assistance and care provided to both applicants in pre-trial detention while on hunger strike in protest against their dismissals from the civil service in the aftermath of the coup attempt of 15 July 2016 • Sufficient efforts made in the prison and the prison hospital to reasonably accommodate the first applicant’s special health needs and ensure he was detained in material conditions compatible with respect for his human dignity and state of health • No evidence that the material conditions of second applicant’s detention in prison and the prison hospital were incompatible with Art 2 or 3

Art 3 (substantive) • Cumulative material conditions of second applicant’s detention at the intensive care unit and the prison ward of a civilian hospital amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment incompatible with her state of health

Art 5 § 1 and Art 5 § 3 • Lawful arrest or detention • Reasonableness of pre-trial detention • Domestic courts’ failure to ensure that the applicants’ pre-trial detention on a suspicion of being members of an armed terrorist organisation was necessary and proportionate and so to dispel fears as to its arbitrariness • Art 15 • No derogating measure applicable to the situation
Prepared by the Registry. Does not bind the Court.
This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.
In the case of Özakça and Gülmen v. Türkiye,
The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:
Arnfinn Bårdsen, President, Saadet Yüksel, Jovan Ilievski, Péter Paczolay, Gediminas Sagatys, Juha Lavapuro, Hugh Mercer, judges, and Andrea Tamietti, Section Registrar,

the applications (nos. 45940/17 and 46171/17) against the Republic of Türkiye lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Turkish nationals, Mr Semih Özakça and Ms Nuriye Gülmen (“the applicants”), on 28 June and 29 June 2017, respectively;
the decision to give notice to the Turkish Government (“the Government”) of the applications;

the decision of 10 July 2017 to give priority to the applications (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court) and the subsequent decision of 20 August 2018 to discontinue the priority treatment of the applications;
the parties’ observations;
Having deliberated in private on 3 November 2026,
Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

1. The applicants are a former teacher and a former academic who went on hunger strike to protest about their dismissal from the civil service by emergency legislative decrees enacted in the aftermath of the attempted coup d’état of 15 July 2016. The case essentially concerns the applicants’ pre-trial detention mainly on a suspicion of being members of an armed terrorist organisation which arose in connection with their protest, and the alleged risk to their lives and physical integrity arising from the deprivation of their liberty despite their fragile health as a result of the hunger strike. The applicants relied on Article 2, Article 3 and Article 5 §§ 1, 3 and 4 of the Convention.

2. The applicants, Mr Semih Özakça (“the first applicant”) and Ms Nuriye Gülmen (“the second applicant”), were born in 1989 and 1982 respectively and the latest information in the case file shows that they live in Ankara. They were initially represented by Mr S. Kozağaçlı, a lawyer practising in Ankara. However, following the arrest and detention of Mr Kozağaçlı on 8 November 2017, they appointed by Mr D.E. Aydın, Ms B. Vangölü Kozağaçlı and Ms Ş. C. Uysal, lawyers practising in Ankara, to represent them before the Court.
3. The Government were represented by their Agent at the time, Mr Hacı Ali Açıkgül, former Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Türkiye.
4. The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.
I. BACKGROUND AND CONTEXT OF THE CASE

5. Following an attempted military coup on 15 July 2016, the Government of Türkiye declared a state of emergency as from 21 July 2016, which remained in force until 18 July 2018 (for further information regarding the military coup attempt and the state of emergency, see Yüksel Yalçınkaya v. Türkiye [GC], no. 15669/20, §§ 10-17, 26 September 2023).

6. On 21 July 2016 the Turkish authorities gave notice to the Secretary General of the Council of Europe of a derogation from the Convention under Article 15 (for the contents of the notice, see Yüksel Yalçınkaya, cited above, § 205). The notice of derogation was withdrawn on 8 August 2018, following the end of the state of emergency.

7. During the state of emergency, the Council of Ministers enacted 37 emergency legislative decrees (nos. 667 to 703) pursuant to Article 121 of the Constitution, bringing in certain emergency measures. On the basis of these legislative decrees, tens of thousands of civil servants were dismissed from their posts, as they were considered to belong to, be affiliated with or linked to (“üyeliǧi, mensubiyeti, iltisakı veya irtibatı”) terrorist organisations or other organisations, structures, or groups which had been deemed by the National Security Council to be engaging in activities detrimental to national security.

8. The Government reported that attacks by various terrorist organisations, which had intensified in the year preceding the coup attempt of 15 July 2016, had continued in full force after that attempt. Between August 2016 and January 2017 alone, more than 240 people were killed and 1,340 people, mostly civilians, were injured as a result of such attacks.
II. THE APPLICANTS’ DISMISSAL FROM THE CIVIL SERVICE AND THEIR DECISION TO GO ON HUNGER STRIKE

9. On 9 September 2016 the first applicant, who at the time was a teacher at a state school in Mardin and a member of a teachers’ union, was suspended from his post. The second applicant, a university academic, was similarly suspended from her post as an assistant professor at the University of Selçuk in Konya on 3 October 2016.

10. On 29 October 2016 and 6 January 2017 respectively, the first and second applicants were dismissed from the civil service by Legislative Decrees nos. 675 and 679, because they belonged to structures which posed a threat to national security or because of their affiliation or links with such structures (see paragraph 7 above). Their passports were revoked by the same legislative decree.

11. On 9 November 2016 the second applicant began holding a sit-in in front of the human rights monument in Ankara, to protest against her suspension. The second applicant was subsequently joined on 23 November 2016 by the first applicant.

12. The applicants’ daily protests attracted considerable attention from the public and the media, both nationally and internationally, and sparked other protests around the country, mostly by persons who had similarly been dismissed from civil service under the legislative decrees. It appears from the information in the case file that during the course of their protests the applicants were taken into police custody approximately 30 times, mainly for acting in contravention of the Meetings and Demonstrations Act (Law no. 2911 – see paragraph 155 below) and resisting the police in the execution of their duties. The case file contains no indication that any of those incidents led to charges resulting in the applicants’ conviction (see also paragraph 15 below).

13. On 9 March 2017 the applicants held a press conference in front of the Turkish Grand National Assembly where they announced that they would start a hunger strike on 11 March 2017 – that is, on the 120th day of their sit‑in – in protest against their allegedly unfair dismissals, and that they would continue it until they were reinstated in their jobs. Following the press conference, the applicants were arrested and taken into police custody by anti‑terrorism police officers (see paragraph 20 et seq. below for the subsequent developments). According to the information provided by the applicants, they began their hunger strike on 9 March 2017 following their arrest.

14. After their release from custody on 14 March 2017 (see paragraph 23 below), the applicants continued with their protest. However, they reduced the duration of their daily sit-ins from 25 March 2017 onwards in view of the deterioration in their health as a result of the hunger strike. From 2 May 2017, they limited their sit-ins to one hour, and no longer held them every day. It appears from the information in the case file that the public gatherings and demonstrations held in protest against the dismissals by legislative decree nevertheless continued in Ankara and elsewhere, even in the applicants’ absence.
III. THE CRIMINAL PROCEEDINGS BROUGHT AGAINST THE APPLICANTS AND THEIR PLACEMENT IN PRE-TRIAL DETENTION

15. As noted in paragraph 12 above, the applicants were taken into police custody on numerous occasions because of their protests. Information in the case file shows that on at least one of those occasions (on 19 November 2017) a criminal investigation was commenced against the second applicant on the charges of participating in an unlawful demonstration and persistently failing to comply with orders of the security forces to disperse (section 32 of the Meetings and Demonstrations Act). However, on 25 April 2017 the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office decided against bringing a prosecution having regard to, inter alia, the fact that the actions took place in an area closed to traffic, involved a limited number of participants, did not depart from peaceful purposes, and were of short duration.

16. Subsequently, two more investigations were commenced against both applicants on suspicion of, inter alia, membership of an armed terrorist organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (“the CC” – see paragraph 153 below). The details of these investigations, and the ensuing criminal proceedings, are outlined below.
A. The first criminal investigation
1. Criminal investigation commenced against the applicants and their detention in police custody

17. On an unspecified date, the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office commenced a criminal investigation into the applicants’ alleged links to an armed terrorist organisation, namely the DHKP/C (People’s Revolutionary Liberation Party/Front) (investigation no. 2017/7560).

18. On 2 February 2017 the Ankara 2nd Magistrates’ Court ordered a restriction of access to the investigation file on the basis of Article 153 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“the CCP”), on the grounds that access could jeopardise the investigation (for the text of the relevant provision, see Yüksekdağ Şenoğlu and Others v. Türkiye, nos. 14332/17 and 12 others, § 441, 8 November 2022).
19. On 7 February 2017 the Ankara 7th Magistrates’ Court made an order in the ongoing investigation for the interception of the applicants’ communications.
20. As stated in paragraph 13 above, on 9 March 2017 the applicants were arrested in Ankara and taken into police custody as part of the first criminal investigation.

21. On the same date a search was carried out at the first applicant’s registered address in Eskişehir, during which the police discovered and seized, inter alia, a number of books and magazines that had been ordered to be confiscated and banned by a court decision. The authorities claimed that those publications were among the materials recommended by the DHKP/C to its supporters; they had been promoted and sold at events organised by bodies affiliated with the organisation in order to generate revenue for the organisation, and contained propaganda in favour of the terrorist organisation and its aims.

22. On 14 March 2017 the applicants were brought before the Ankara chief public prosecutor. The first applicant stated that since there had been no collective action by his trade union against the mass dismissals from civil service, he had decided to stage an individual protest and had therefore joined the second applicant, whose protests he had become aware of through the press and the internet. He maintained that he had undertaken the protest on his own initiative, with the aim of making his voice heard following his dismissal, and denied having acted at the direction of the DHKP/C or any other organisation. The second applicant made a similar statement.

23. Later on the same day, the applicants appeared before the Ankara 2nd Magistrates’ Court with their lawyers, where they essentially repeated the statements they had previously made to the public prosecutor. Having regard to the evidence in the case file, the magistrate found that there was a strong suspicion that the applicants had committed the offence of membership of an armed terrorist organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the CC (see paragraph 153 below). The magistrate did not, however, consider it necessary to order the applicants’ pre-trial detention and instead decided to place them under judicial supervision pursuant to Article 109 § 3 (b) of the CCP (see paragraph 158 below). The applicants were therefore required to report to their local police station once a week, which they duly did. They also continued with their daily sit-in protests and hunger strike following their release (see paragraph 14 above).

24. On 17 March 2017 the applicants were arrested and taken into police custody once again on the same grounds and in connection with the same protest. On 19 March 2017 the Ankara public prosecutor’s office ordered their release in view of the judicial supervision measure already in place.
2. Bill of indictment of 2 May 2017

25. On 2 May 2017 the Ankara public prosecutor’s office filed a bill of indictment (“the first bill of indictment”) with the Ankara 19th Assize Court (“the trial court”) against the applicants, and one other person who had participated in the sit-in, namely A.K. The applicants were charged with membership of an armed terrorist organisation, namely the DHKP/C, under Article 314 § 2 of the CC, and with disseminating propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation, under section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) (see paragraphs 153 and 154 below).

26. The indictment first outlined the structure of the DHKP/C terrorist organisation, the bodies affiliated with it, its methods of operation and its previous activities. It then described the investigation. In this connection, it noted that many protests and other events such as those carried out by the applicants had taken place in Ankara since November 2016. Those events were allegedly organised by the “open-area” formations of the DHKP/C, including the “Revolutionary Civil Servants’ Movement” (Devrimci Memur Hareketi), which the authorities considered to be the terrorist organisation’s ostensibly legal structure which operated among civil servants. The events were said to have been held in response to an article published on 23 October 2016 in Yürüyüş, a magazine allegedly affiliated with that organisation, calling for protests against the state of emergency, the legislative decrees and alleged human rights violations in Türkiye. According to the bill of indictment, those protests and related events were not carried out in pursuit of democratic rights but were organised on the instructions of the terrorist organisation, to motivate its followers and to further the organisation’s aims.

27. The applicants, who were allegedly operating within the Revolutionary Civil Servants’ Movement, were said to have taken an active role in those events by reading out press statements, addressing and sometimes directing the crowd, and chanting slogans. In support of the argument that the applicants had carried out the acts alleged on the instructions of the terrorist organisation DHKP/C, the bill of indictment referred to certain publications in magazines, on websites and in social media accounts affiliated with the DHKP/C. These publications expressed support for the applicants’ protests, describing them as connected to or as continuations of past acts of civil disobedience or resistance against the Government carried out by the DHKP/C (including hunger strikes). The publications portrayed the applicants as being identified with the DHKP/C and calling for broader resistance. The publications emphasised that past acts of resistance carried out by certain late members of the DHKP/C – described as “martyrs” – had achieved success and that the same success would be achieved by the resistance undertaken by the applicants, so presenting them as associated with the organisation.

28. Concerning specifically the applicants’ activities, the public prosecutor pointed to the similarities between their methods of protest and those used by the DHKP/C, and referred in the bill of indictment to the following activities undertaken between November 2016 and February 2017:

- social media posts by the applicants reporting on their daily demonstrations and expressing support for other protestors, and the sharing of those posts by accounts believed to be affiliated with the DHKP/C;

- other social media activities by the applicants, reproducing or referring to material originating from accounts or groups believed to be associated with the DHKP/C or other illegal organisations, and expressing support for individuals or other actors and entities considered to belong to, or be affiliated with, the DHKP/C;

- records of telephone conversations between the second applicant and representatives of various local and Europe-based media outlets apparently at the request of the media outlets, which wanted to report on the second applicant and the protests;
- further records of telephone conversations with individuals about their protests and about invitations to attend other events;

- the applicants’ participation on 28 January 2017 in a meeting referred to as the “Elmas Yalçın Congress” organised by the Revolutionary Civil Servants’ Movement to draw attention to the unfair dismissal of civil servants by legislative decree, and the advertising of this event in magazines and social media accounts considered to be associated with the DHKP/C;
- the applicants’ chanting of the slogan “we are workers, we are right, we will win” (işçiyiz, haklıyız, kazanacağız) which was associated with the DHKP/C;
- the banned material seized from the first applicant’s registered address (see paragraph 21 above), which was considered to be propaganda for the DHKP/C.

29. On 23 May 2017 the Ankara 19th Assize Court accepted the bill of indictment filed by the public prosecutor against the applicants and A.K. and the case file was registered under case no. 2017/137 E.

30. In its preliminary report (tensip zaptı) issued on the same day, the Ankara 19th Assize Court set the date of the first hearing and ordered the applicants and A.K. to be present for the hearing. The court observed in its report that the applicants were in in pre-trial detention in connection with another offence.
B. The second criminal investigation
1. Criminal investigation commenced against the applicants and their placement in pre-trial detention

31. It appears from the information in the case file that on 21 May 2017 a further criminal investigation was commenced concerning the applicants’ protests, apparently covering the period from 2 May 2017 – that is, the date of the filing of the first bill of indictment (see paragraph 25 above and paragraph 50 below).

32. On the same day the Anti-Terrorism Branch of the Ankara Security Directorate asked the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office for authorisation to conduct a search of the applicants’ place of residence in Ankara, to seize any incriminating material and to arrest them. It was noted in the request that, following the dismissal of certain individuals active within the Revolutionary Civil Servants’ Movement from the civil service, press statements had been made and sit-in protests had been organised in Ankara under the auspices of that movement from November 2016 onward. In that context, a criminal investigation had been opened against the applicants for suspected membership of the DHKP/C and subsequently criminal proceedings were begun against them in the Ankara 19th Assize Court under case no. 2017/137 E (see paragraph 29 above). The request continued as follows:

“[It has been noted that the applicants] continued their protest without interruption with the support of the open-area structures of the DHKP/C terrorist organisation, that they rented a house in ... Ankara, that they could continue their protest in that house under the name ‘Death Fast Resistance House’, that by 21 May 2017 [the applicants] had been on hunger strike for seventy-four days, ... that the said [strike] ... had evolved from an allegedly legitimate demand into an activity serving the organisation’s recruitment efforts and aimed at mobilising its sympathisers, that if the protest were to continue the hunger strike might be turned into a ‘death fast’, which could then be exploited by the organisation for propaganda purposes in the event of the protesters’ deaths, that it was known that the DHKP/C terrorist organisation had previously resorted to similar actions and that the protest had also been supported by other radical left-wing groups in an attempt to attract broader public attention and mobilise larger crowds, that the [Ankara chief] public prosecutor’s office had been informed that this was possibly being done with a view to escalating these protests into violent events similar to the TEKEL workers’ protests in Ankara and the Gezi events[1], and that instructions had been received [from the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office] for ‘Nuriye Gülmen and Semih Özakça to be apprehended and taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of a terrorist organisation ...”
33. The Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office granted the Security Directorate’s request on the same date.

34. On the night of 22 May 2017, a search was therefore conducted in the flat that the applicants had rented together in Ankara, which the authorities referred to as the “Death Fast Resistance House”. During this search, the police officers seized, inter alia, several books and magazines, which were considered to be affiliated with, and promoted by, the DHKP/C.
35. On 23 May 2017 at 2.00 a.m., following the search of the house, the applicants were taken into police custody.

36. Subsequently on the same day, the applicants were taken to the Ankara chief public prosecutor’s office, where they made statements in the presence of their lawyers. The first applicant repeated that he had joined the second applicant’s protest as a reaction to his dismissal from civil service. His only goal was to be reinstated to his post; the fact that their protest had later been taken up or supported by other individuals or organisations was not a matter over which he and the second applicant had had any control. He added that he had personal Twitter and Facebook accounts and that he had occasionally seen posts about himself shared or tagged on other social media accounts, and had sometimes reposted those which concerned him. He maintained that he was neither a member nor an affiliate of any terrorist organisation, and that he had not carried out any protest or action on behalf of any organisation. Lastly, he stated that the house where they had been on hunger strike had been rented by his spouse and that their needs there had been covered by their respective families; no support had been received from unlawful groups or organisations.

37. The second applicant made a statement to similar effect. When asked by the public prosecutor whether she was aware of the efforts by the DHKP/C and its affiliates to make use of her protest, including by publishing news about it or issuing calls to action in connection with it, the applicant reiterated that her sole aim was to protest against her dismissal; the fact that many people, like her, had been unlawfully dismissed from their jobs by legislative decree was not something for which she was responsible. She added that many passers-by had expressed support for their protests and their cause. She maintained that the support for their demands for reinstatement could not be attributed to the encouragement or direction of any organisation.

38. Following the questioning, the public prosecutor applied to the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court for an order for the applicants’ pre-trial detention on the grounds that they were suspected of (i) membership of an armed terrorist organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the CC (see paragraph 153 below) and of (ii) having acted in contravention of section 34 of the Meetings and Demonstrations Act by inciting or encouraging the public to participate in unlawful assemblies (see paragraph 155 below). The prosecutor observed that although his office had commenced criminal proceedings against them (see, in respect of the first investigation, the indictment dated 2 May 2017, summarised in paragraph 25 above), the applicants had continued their activities, on the instructions of the DHKP/C and its affiliates. Under the guise of protesting against their dismissal from the public service, they had, therefore, continued to act on behalf of the organisation and to contribute to its recruitment efforts. The prosecutor claimed in this regard that the applicants’ activities had evolved into demonstrations by which they aimed to bring pressure on the authorities, and that they had encouraged the public to take part in unlawful demonstrations.

39. On 23 May 2017 the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office also applied for restrictions to be put on the defence’s rights to examine the case file and to obtain copies of documents under Article 153 § 2 of the CCP (see paragraph 18 above), on the grounds that it could jeopardise the investigation. The application was granted by the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court on the same day.

40. Still on the same day, the applicants were brought before the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court on an application for their pre-trial detention on the charges set out in paragraph 38 above. The second applicant reiterated that she had initiated the protest with the legitimate aim of regaining her job and that others with the same demand had subsequently joined her. She argued that the accusation of membership of a terrorist organisation had arisen after her protest had attracted significant public support, and pointed out that many people had been dismissed by legislative decree in similar circumstances. She maintained that she had not acted at the direction of any organisation, had not displayed any unlawful banners, and had not engaged in any propaganda for an illegal organisation, and there was no record of her engaging in such activity. She further considered her detention to be an attempt to force her to end her protest and her hunger strike.

41. The second applicant’s lawyers emphasised that although the authorities had tried to link her to the DHKP/C, her protest had in fact received support from many different NGOs, had been widely covered by the press, and had even been discussed during a session of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (see paragraph 164 below). They also said that her protest had involved no illegal activity and that the latest accusations against her were based on a small number of social media posts selectively presented to the court, whereas thousands of other social media posts by people from various walks of life expressing support for her could have been produced. The lawyers requested the magistrate to take into consideration that since 2 May 2017, the second applicant had been able to pursue her sit-in for only one hour a day, and not even every day, because of her state of health; the protests had nevertheless continued at full force. The protesters were individuals who, like the applicants, had been dismissed from the civil service by legislative decree but had not engaged in a hunger strike, which the lawyers claimed supported the view that the applicants’ detention was aimed specifically at bringing their hunger strike to an end. Lastly, they stressed that the applicant had fully complied with the earlier order for judicial supervision (see paragraph 23 above) and that there were therefore no grounds for detaining her pending trial, as also evidenced by the prosecutor’s decision not to detain her after she was taken into police custody on 17 March 2017 in respect of the same protest (see paragraph 24 above). Her detention now in her current state of health could lead to irreparable harm.

42. The first applicant made a statement along similar lines. His lawyers claimed that the accusations against both applicants were based on the support shown on social media accounts or websites affiliated with the DHPK/C, whereas associating the applicants with that organisation on the basis of whom it supported or whose photographs it shared was wholly unfounded. They emphasised that thousands of people had rallied in support of the applicants’ protests. The lawyers also questioned the reasons for seeking the applicants’ detention within the framework of the second investigation, observing that the previous investigation had lasted for many months and had resulted in a bill of indictment (see paragraphs 17-24 above), but had not necessitated their pre-trial detention. Both the applicant and his lawyers contended in that regard that the real aim behind the application for his detention was to stop the hunger strike. They lastly drew the court’s attention to the applicant’s state of health, which they claimed was at risk of seriously deteriorating if he remained in detention.

43. On 23 May 2017 the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court ordered the applicants to be placed in pre-trial detention pursuant to Article 100 et. seq. of the CCP (see paragraphs 156 and 157 below). The magistrate found a strong suspicion that the applicants had committed the offences of which they were accused, observing that they had persisted in their activities on behalf of the DHKP/C despite the commencement of criminal proceedings against them under an indictment dated 2 May 2017 (see paragraphs 25-28 above), and taking also into account their activity on social media platforms and photographs.

44. In justifying the applicants’ pre-trial detention, the magistrate referred to the nature of the offence of membership of a terrorist organisation with which they were charged, noting that it constituted a “catalogue offence” under Article 100 § 3 of the CCP (that is, an offence for which there was a statutory presumption of grounds for detention, see paragraph 156 below), and also referred to the minimum and maximum statutory penalties for that offence. The magistrate further stated that a decision not to place the applicants in pre-trial detention would hinder the proper administration of justice, as not all the evidence against them had yet been collected, and concluded that alternative preventive measures, such as judicial supervision, would be insufficient in the circumstances.

45. On the same day the magistrates’ court made two separate pre-trial detention orders (tutuklama müzekkeresi) for each applicant, one relating to the offence of membership of an armed terrorist organisation and the other to the offence of inciting or encouraging the public to participate in unlawful assemblies. The detention orders were carried out only in respect of the former offence, that is, membership of an armed terrorist organisation (see paragraph 99 below for the information provided in the Constitutional Court’s judgment in this regard). The applicants were placed at the Ankara Sincan Closed Prison (“the Sincan Prison”).

46. On 24 May 2017 the applicants objected to the pre-trial detention orders in the Ankara 6th Magistrate’s Court. They argued that the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court had failed to demonstrate any risk that they might abscond or interfere with evidence and had not explained why alternative preventive measures would be insufficient. They were already under judicial supervision in the context of another ongoing investigation relating to the same protest, and they had complied with the requirements of that order by reporting regularly to the authorities (see paragraph 23 above). The applicants further claimed there was no evidence capable of giving rise to a strong suspicion that they had committed an offence. They asserted that it was not possible to establish any link with the DHKP/C on the basis of posts made by third parties on the internet or to draw conclusions as to the purpose of those posts. They maintained in this regard that their protests had been supported by numerous persons and institutions, both nationally and internationally. In any event, the social media posts in question had not carried any content that would constitute a criminal offence. The applicants lastly stated that their detention was disproportionate as they were on the 75th day of their hunger strike and were in a critical condition, which would further deteriorate because of the conditions of detention. They also expressed their concerns that the detention order had been made to enable their force-feeding, since forced intervention was only possible for persons held in detention.
47. There is no information in the case file as to how the Ankara 6th Magistrates’ Court dealt with the applicants’ objections to the detention orders.

48. On 31 May 2017 the applicants again applied to be released, this time to the Ankara 19th Assize Court. They drew the court’s attention to the fact that while detention had not been considered necessary in respect of the first investigation concerning protests spanning nearly 160 days, the second investigation – relating only to a 21-day period (between 2 May and 22 May 2017) during which the same acts had been carried out – had led to their detention. They considered this to be unjustified and disproportionate, as well as a misuse of detention. They claimed that their state of health constituted a further indication of the disproportionate nature of detention.
49. The Ankara 19th Assize Court considered the applicants’ arguments on 5 June 2017, when it ordered the joinder of the two sets of criminal proceedings against them (see paragraph 54 below).
2. Bill of indictment of 24 May 2017

50. On 24 May 2017 the Ankara public prosecutor’s office filed another bill of indictment (“the second bill of indictment”) with the Ankara 19th Assize Court, this time only against the two applicants. It concerned their activities between 2 May and 24 May 2017, that is, after the filing of the first indictment on 2 May 2017 (see paragraphs 25 and 31 above). In the bill of indictment, the public prosecutor charged the applicants with membership of an armed terrorist organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the CC (see paragraph 153 below) and with inciting or encouraging the public to participate in unlawful assemblies under Article 34 of the Meetings and Demonstrations Act (see paragraph 155 below).

51. Following an overview of the history and activities of DHKP/C and its connection to the Revolutionary Civil Servants’ Movement, the second bill of indictment set out the prosecutor’s findings regarding the alleged links between the applicants’ activities and the DHKP/C, based on material similar in type and nature to that referred to in the first bill of indictment (see paragraphs 26-28 above). It was argued that at the time of their dismissal from civil service the applicants were operating within the Revolutionary Civil Servants’ Movement. Moreover, the applicants’ choice of protest, namely a hunger strike, was one that had commonly been used by the DHKP/C and other left-wing terrorist organisations since the 1980s. It was claimed that the purpose of this particular type of protest was to exert public pressure on the State to accept the protestors’ demands and to maintain organisational cohesion by boosting morale and motivation and recruiting new members. The applicants had also tried to use their hunger strike to gain support on social media, in the national media and internationally.

52. The bill of indictment observed that despite the deterioration in the applicants’ health, in particular that of the second applicant, they were pursuing their hunger strike and were not accepting medical intervention. It concluded as follows:

“When the suspects’ actions and the expressions of support for those actions are assessed together, it is understood that the actions carried out by the suspects were characteristic of the DHKP/C terrorist organisation; that those actions were organised nationwide by the organisation; that the actions carried out across the country were endorsed on websites and social media accounts affiliated with the organisation, where calls for support were also made and backing was provided by individuals and structures sympathetic to the organisation; that the actions carried out by the suspects were initiated and sustained on the instructions of the terrorist organisation; and that they therefore cannot be regarded as innocent actions in defence of rights. It is further understood that, should the actions continue, any deterioration in the condition of potential participants would lead to the State being held responsible and that, [the intention was to] escalate these actions into Gezi-type uprisings.”
53. The public prosecutor requested that the case be joined with case no. 2017/13 E. pending before the Ankara 19th Assize Court (see paragraph 29 above).

54. On 5 June 2017 the trial court ordered the joinder of the two sets of criminal proceedings against the applicants under case no. 2017/137 E., on the grounds that both proceedings concerned the same offences and the same defendants. In the same decision, the assize court also ordered the applicants’ continued detention. In taking this decision, the court considered the nature of the offence of which the applicants were accused, namely membership of an armed terrorist organisation, and the penalty for that offence; the state of the evidence; the existence of concrete evidence indicating a strong suspicion that the offence had been committed; the fact that the offence fell within the catalogue of offences listed in Article 100 § 3 of the CCP (see paragraph 156 below); and the time the applicants had already spent in detention. It held on that basis that judicial supervision would be insufficient at this stage.

55. On 8 June 2017 the applicants lodged an objection to the trial court’s order for their detention, essentially along similar lines to those of their previous objections (see paragraph 46 above). They added that the Ankara Medical Association (Ankara Tabip Odası), which had monitored their hunger strike since its outset, had requested permission from the Ministry of Justice to continue monitoring their health in detention, but that this request had been refused (see paragraph 103 below). As they had not been allowed to exercise their right to choose their own doctors and had therefore refused to be examined by the physicians at the prison complex, they were continuing the hunger strike without medical supervision.

56. On 13 June 2017 the Ankara 20th Assize Court rejected the objection, citing the same reasons as the trial court (as noted in paragraph 54 above). The assize court stated that the applicants’ pre-trial detention was based on the offence of “membership of an armed terrorist organisation”. It did not mention the offence under section 34 of the Meetings and Demonstrations Act (see paragraph 155 below).

57. On 22 June 2017 the applicants applied to the Ankara 20th Assize Court, challenging the independence and impartiality of the trial court and requesting the recusal of the judges who heard their case. Firstly, they contended that the trial court’s decision to accept the first bill of indictment on 23 May 2017 (see paragraph 29 above) had provided the material foundation for the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court to make its subsequent detention order, which was based on the allegation that the applicants had persisted in their activities notwithstanding the commencement of criminal proceedings against them (see paragraph 43 above). In the applicants’ view, the timing of the trial court’s decision raised doubts as to its independence. They secondly submitted that in its request for their arrest on 21 May 2017 (see paragraph 32 above), the Ankara Security Directorate had referred to the criminal proceedings before the trial court together with the case number, even though the first bill of indictment had not then been accepted by the trial court and no case number had been assigned to it at that stage. This, in the applicants’ view, indicated that the judicial process was effectively being steered by the police rather than by the trial court. The applicants lastly argued that in its preliminary report following the acceptance of the bill of indictment, the trial court had referred to them as being in pre-trial detention (see paragraph 30 above), even though the detention order had not yet been made by the magistrates’ court at that point.

58. On 23 June 2017 the trial court informed the Ankara 20th Assize Court that the contested reference in their preliminary report to the applicants as being in pre-trial detention had been a clerical error. There is no information in the case file as to the decision delivered by the Ankara 20th Assize Court in response to the applicants’ objection.

59. On 30 June, 28 July and 25 August 2017 the trial court made an order of its own motion extending the applicants’ pre-trial detention on suspicion of membership of an armed terrorist organisation, giving the same reasons as in its previous decision (see paragraph 54 above). It also observed that under the case-law of the European Court of Human Rights the protection of public order and the prevention of the commission of further offences constituted legitimate grounds for detention and that the applicants presented a risk of absconding or tampering with evidence if they were released. The applicants’ objections to these decisions were dismissed by the Ankara 20th Assize Court.

60. On 28 July 2017 both applicants were transferred from the Sincan prison to the State hospital within the Sincan prison complex (“the Sincan prison hospital”) (see paragraph 126 below for further information on the medical reasons underlying this transfer). Subsequently on 26 September 2017, the second applicant was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit (“the ICU”) of the Ankara Numune Training and Research Hospital (“the Numune Hospital”), a fully-equipped civilian hospital, and on 9 October 2017, to the prison ward of the Numune Hospital (see paragraphs 140 and 147 below, respectively).

61. On 14 September 2017 a first hearing was held before the Ankara 19th Assize Court. The trial court was informed by the Sincan prison authorities that the applicants could not be present at the hearing because of the state of their health, as well as because of a lack of personnel to ensure the security of the proceedings.

62. At the hearing the trial court heard from, inter alios, the heads of the Ankara, Van, Adana, Antalya and Sakarya Bar Associations, who spoke in support of the defence. These lawyers reiterated that the applicants had carried out their protest for a legitimate and lawful purpose, namely to seek reinstatement in their jobs. Their means of protest, namely a hunger strike, was an exercise of their freedom of expression; they had not engaged in any violent acts and had received support from all those who had similarly lost their jobs by legislative decree. The lawyers added that in view of the condition of their health, which severely limited their ability to move, there was no risk that the applicants would abscond or interfere with evidence as alleged, and they asked for the applicants’ release.

63. At the close of the hearing, the trial court ordered the applicants’ continued detention on suspicion of membership of an armed terrorist organisation, having regard to the nature of that offence as a “catalogue offence” (see paragraph 44 above and paragraph 156 below) and to the minimum and maximum penalties prescribed by law for that offence. It found that detention was proportionate to the potential sentence and that, as the evidence had not yet been fully collected, there was a risk that it might be destroyed, concealed or altered. It also referred to the medical report submitted to it by the Numune Hospital on an unspecified date, which indicated that the applicants’ health did not preclude their detention. The trial court ordered the submission of all reports and other documents relating to the applicants’ medical condition.

64. The second hearing was held on 28 September 2017. The first applicant was brought to the court from the Sincan prison hospital for the hearing. However, the second applicant could not be present. A medical report from the Numune Hospital said that her participation would be medically ill-advised.

65. The applicants’ lawyers asked for the applicants’ release and complained about the conditions in the hospitals where they were being held against their will. The first applicant mainly complained that there was insufficient ventilation and sunlight at the Sincan prison hospital and that he had not had a family member at the hospital to assist him (refakatçi) for an extended period of time (see paragraphs 138-139 below). He also added that they had been detained pre-emptively, because of the fear that their protest might generate wider protests similar to the Gezi events.

66. The second applicant’s lawyers stated that in the ICU she was held in her room all day and was required to use a commode chair, placed next to the bed, as a toilet; the door to her room remained open at all times, with gendarmerie officers posted outside (see paragraph 143 below for further details on the conditions of detention in the ICU). She had also been deprived of any assistance and was not even able to change her clothes.

67. The lawyers contended that the longer the applicants remained in detention while on hunger strike, the greater the risk of forced medical intervention such as force-feeding, which could have extremely serious consequences. They explained that the applicants were refusing medical treatment because no relationship of trust could be built with the doctors at the prison hospital and the Numune Hospital, who were allegedly threatening to force-feed them.

68. The lawyers also repeated the allegation that the applicants had been deprived of their liberty to force them to end their hunger strike and that there were no grounds justifying their detention. They argued that the applicants had been detained despite the judicial supervision measure already in place for the same offence and the same actions, and stressed that an earlier attempt to detain them on 19 March 2017 had been turned down because of that supervision (see paragraph 24 above). In the absence of any new evidence or arguments, their detention on 23 May 2017 was completely unjustified and was tainted by irregularities. They reiterated in this regard that when requesting their arrest on 21 May 2017 (see paragraph 32 above), the Ankara Security Directorate had referred to the criminal proceedings in the trial, although those proceedings had only commenced, and a case number had only been assigned, with the acceptance of the bill of indictment on 23 May 2017 (see paragraph 29 above).

69. The lawyers further informed the court that despite the applicants’ absence, the protests of individuals who had similarly been dismissed from civil service by legislative decree were continuing. The applicants’ detention had therefore not achieved the unlawful aim of suppressing protest, as had been intended by the authorities.

70. In her statement to the trial court, the applicants’ co-defendant A.K. similarly argued that the applicants had been detained solely because of their hunger strike, pointing out that she herself had not participated in the hunger strike and had remained at liberty, despite facing the same charges for engaging in the same sit-in protest.

71. At that hearing, the trial court also heard a medical expert who had been called to give evidence by the applicants. The medical expert emphasised the vital importance of regular monitoring of persons on hunger strike and stated that, although such monitoring had been ensured by the Ankara Medical Association prior to the applicants’ detention, the applicants had since refused monitoring and treatment in protest against their detention.

72. At the end of the hearing, the trial court decided to extend the applicants’ pre-trial detention, repeating the reasons given at the close of the first hearing (see paragraph 63 above). The court also referred to the witness evidence given by a certain B.E. in the context of a separate set of criminal proceedings, in which B.E. had claimed that the applicants were pursuing the hunger strike on the DHKP/C’s instructions (see paragraphs 79 and 80 below). The court lastly requested a report from the Numune Hospital on whether the second applicant’s medical condition constituted an obstacle to her continued detention.

73. On 10 October 2017 the Numune Hospital informed the trial court that the commission established by the hospital administration to oversee the second applicant’s monitoring and treatment found her to be in a life-threatening condition. It was, however, concluded that there was no medical condition preventing her detention, as all necessary examinations, tests and treatment could be carried out, with her consent, in the hospital ward designated for detainees, where she was then being held.

74. In a separate report made on the same day the Numune Hospital said that it would not be appropriate for the second applicant to participate in the hearing. Her current condition was life-threatening and she was refusing the recommended examinations and tests, which had made any further objective medical assessment impossible. The hospital therefore advised the trial court to take her defence statement at the hospital.

75. At the third hearing, which was held on 12 October 2017, the trial court decided to obtain the second applicant’s statement at the hospital as advised. On 16 October 2017 the three judges of the Ankara 19th Assize Court hearing the applicants’ case, together with the public prosecutor and the applicants’ lawyers, therefore went to the Numune Hospital to take her statement.

76. The second applicant complained to the trial court about the conditions of her detention, first in the ICU and then on the prison ward of the Numune Hospital where she had been transferred on 9 October 2017 (see paragraph 60 above). She mainly repeated the arguments about the conditions in the ICU that had been raised by her lawyers at the second hearing and subsequently before the Court, in particular as regards the difficulties she faced when using the toilet, which she argued amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment (see paragraph 66 above and paragraph 143 below). She stated that following her demands she had eventually managed to have a screen placed in front of the toilet chair, but that still did not provide her with the required privacy given that she was under constant supervision from the gendarmerie officers and that anyone could walk into the room whenever they wished. She also complained that she was deprived of the assistance of an accompanying family member in the ICU and that she had not been able to have a shower during her detention there.

77. As for the conditions on the prison ward of the Numune Hospital to which she was subsequently transferred, she claimed that she was being held in a basement room where there was no natural light, to the point that it was not possible to distinguish day from night, where the lights were permanently on, including during the night, where there was no access to fresh air and the ventilation was wholly insufficient and extremely loud. She argued that these conditions, which prevented her from sleeping, amounted to torture, given in particular her frail state of health as a result of her hunger strike. She stated that even those sentenced to life imprisonment were detained in better conditions, with access to fresh air at least one hour per day. She confirmed, however, that her sister had been allowed to accompany her at the Numune Hospital (see paragraph 206 below).
4. The remaining hearings and the judgment of the trial court

78. The Ankara 19th Assize Court held four more hearings after the third one. The first applicant was present at all the hearings, but the second applicant participated from the hospital via the SEGBİS sound and image information system (Ses ve Görüntü Bilişim Sistemi), as the Numune Hospital had advised against her attending in person because of her state of health.

79. During the proceedings, the trial court heard a number of witnesses, including a prosecution witness, B.E. (see paragraph 72 above). He had given information about the DHKP/C and its activities as a defendant in separate criminal proceedings for membership of the organisation, in order to benefit from the “active repentance” provision in the CC, which allowed for a reduction of sentence in exchange for information. B.E. had made an initial statement to the Istanbul Public Prosecutor’s Office on 19 July 2017, where he had stated that the applicants were conducting their hunger strike under the direction of the DHKP/C and alleged that he had seen the terrorist organisation’s written instructions in that regard. When he was subsequently heard by the Ankara 19th Assize Court at the fourth hearing on 20 October 2017, however, he retracted that statement and told the trial court that he had no direct information as to whether the applicants had conducted their hunger strike under the organisation’s direction or not.

80. B.E. further claimed that while he did not have organisational ties with the first applicant and had no concrete information about him, he had personally witnessed the second applicant making contact with members of the DHKP/C back as far as 2012. He also said that in 2014 he had met with the second applicant – together with a certain F.S. and a certain Ö.L.Z., who were also heard at the hearing – to prepare a simple explosive device for use at a protest about the death of a minor during the Gezi events in Istanbul (see Elvan v. Türkiye, no. 64937/19, 7 February 2023 for the application introduced in relation to the death of the minor in question, namely Berkin Elvan). While F.S. confirmed this claim to the trial court, Ö.L.Z. denied it. The second applicant admitted to having participated in the protest in question in 2014 but denied having prepared any explosive device. The witnesses called by the defence confirmed her participation in the protest but stated that they did not see her use any explosives or engage in other unlawful acts. They also submitted that the applicants had initiated the hunger strike as a genuine protest against their dismissal, and not because they were acting on the instructions of any illegal organisation.

81. At the fourth hearing, which was held on 20 October 2017, the trial court ordered the first applicant’s release, subject to restrictions under Article 109 § 3 (j) of the CCP, namely a requirement not to leave his residence, also known as “house arrest” (see paragraph 158 below). The second applicant’s lawyers insisted on her release because of her deteriorating health condition. However, the trial court decided to extend her detention on suspicion of membership of an armed terrorist organisation for the reasons given at the close of the first hearing (see paragraph 63 above).

82. At each hearing, the second applicant continued to complain about the conditions of her detention on the Numune Hospital prison ward. She claimed, in particular, that she had not been allowed to go out for fresh air since her admission onto the prison ward on 9 October 2017 (see paragraph 60 above) and that there was no properly functioning ventilation (see also the complaints made by the second applicant at the third hearing, summarised in paragraph 77 above).

83. At the sixth hearing, which was held on 27 November 2017, the public prosecutor requested the second applicant’s release from detention, subject to judicial supervision measures as the trial court saw fit. In support of the request, he referred to the fact that all the evidence in the case file had already been gathered, the absence of any risk of the applicant tampering with the evidence or absconding, and the stage reached in the proceedings. At the close of the hearing, the trial court rejected the public prosecutor’s request and decided to extend the second applicant’s pre-trial detention because of the strong suspicion that she had committed the offence of membership of an armed terrorist organisation, the classification of that offence as a “catalogue offence” under Article 100 § 3 of the CCP (see paragraphs 44 and 63 above and paragraph 156 below), and the maximum penalty prescribed for that offence.

84. At the seventh hearing, which was held on 1 December 2017, the Ankara 19th Assize Court delivered its judgment, acquitting the first applicant on all charges. It noted, in particular, that there was no solid and convincing evidence, beyond reasonable doubt, that the first applicant had carried out his hunger strike on the orders and instructions of the DHKP/C.

85. As for the second applicant, the trial court convicted her of membership of an armed terrorist organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the CC (see paragraph 153 below) and sentenced her to six years and three months’ imprisonment. The trial court held that there was similarly no solid evidence to show beyond reasonable doubt that the second applicant had initiated and carried out her hunger strike under the direction of the DHKP/C. It found, nevertheless, that her membership of that terrorist organisation had been proved by the actions described in the statements of the witnesses B.E. and F.S. (see paragraph 80 above). It acquitted her on all the remaining charges.

86. The trial court also ordered the second applicant’s release, subject to a ban on leaving the country, having regard to the delivery of its judgment, the time that she had spent in detention, the absence of any risk of absconding at that stage of the proceedings, and the length of the sentence imposed.
87. On 11 June 2020 the Ankara Regional Court of Appeal upheld the trial court’s judgment in respect of both applicants.
88. According to the information provided by the Government on 15 April 2026, on that date the proceedings were still pending before the Court of Cassation.
IV. PROCEEDINGS IN THE CONSTITUTIONAL COURT
A. The applicants’ individual application to the Constitutional Court and their application for an interim order

89. On 22 June 2017, while the criminal proceedings were still pending in the trial court, the applicants lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court, complaining, inter alia, of a violation of their rights to life and personal integrity (Article 17 of the Constitution) and to liberty and security (Article 19 of the Constitution), their right to a fair trial (Article 36 of the Constitution), their right to freedom of expression (Article 26 of the Constitution) and their right to freedom of assembly (Article 34 of the Constitution). The applicants’ complaints concerning the right to life and personal integrity and the right to liberty and security largely corresponded to those subsequently raised before the Court under Articles 2, 3 and 5 of the Convention (see paragraphs 195 and 256 below), with the exception of their complaint under Article 5 § 4 concerning the restriction of access to the investigation file (see paragraphs 307 and 314 below). In their application to the Constitutional Court, the applicants argued that the restriction in question had prevented them from ascertaining whether the prosecution had collected any evidence in their favour, and had thus prevented them from preparing their defence, in violation of their right to a fair trial. They did not argue that the restriction had hindered their ability to challenge the legality of their detention.

90. The applicants also asked the Constitutional Court to make an interim order for their immediate release from detention, in view of the real risk of permanent disability or death arising from their detention while on hunger strike. They argued in this regard that they were experiencing, inter alia, low blood pressure and slowed pulse, headaches, stomach pain, muscle pain, difficulty walking, oral lesions, and sensitivity to light and noise. They stated that, since the beginning of the hunger strike, the first applicant had lost 24 kilograms and the second applicant 12 kilograms.

91. The applicants acknowledged that the risks they referred to were primarily caused by the hunger strike, which they had begun themselves and which they were continuing voluntarily as an exercise of their freedom of expression. They claimed, however, that while they had been able, as individuals at liberty, to weigh that risk against their interest in exercising that freedom, their deprivation of liberty had removed that capacity. They argued in this regard that the real, and illegitimate, purpose of detaining them was to force them to end their hunger strike through force-feeding, as provided for under section 82 (2) Law no. 5275 on the enforcement of sentences and preventive measures (see paragraph 159 below), which could only be used while a person was in detention. This, in the applicants’ view, was evidenced by the fact that their co-defendant A.K., who had engaged in exactly the same actions as them except for the hunger strike, had not been taken into pre-trial detention.

92. In support of their application for an interim order, the applicants also argued that being placed in detention had effectively removed their right to choose their own doctors. The authorities’ rejection of their request to continue their hunger strike under the medical supervision of the Ankara Medical Association (see paragraph 55 above) had led the applicants to refuse medical treatment by the prison doctors, resulting in their health remaining entirely unmonitored.

93. The applicants referred to the expert report prepared by the Human Rights Committee of the Turkish Medical Association (Türk Tabipleri Birliği İnsan Hakları Kurulu) (see paragraph 107 below) and further submitted that the physical conditions in the prison where they were being held had aggravated the risk arising from the hunger strike.
B. The Constitutional Court’s decision on the applicants’ application for an interim order

94. On receiving the applicants’ request for an interim order, the Constitutional Court asked the prisons where they were being held to say whether the Council of Forensic Medicine had issued a report on the compatibility of the applicants’ state of health with being held in detention and, if not, whether the applicants had requested such a report. It also asked for information on the monitoring and treatment of the applicants; on whether they had access to emergency medical care if required; and on their conditions of detention.

95. The prisons informed the Constitutional Court that while there had been no request from the applicants, arrangements had been made to transfer them to the Forensic Medicine Institute for medical examination. In the meantime, the first applicant had informed the authorities in writing that he would refuse to be examined by the prison doctors and would not agree to any treatment other than that prescribed by the Ankara Medical Association. He had also refused to be transferred to the State hospital within the prison complex. Nevertheless, he had been provided with vitamins, sugar and fluids by the prison doctor. He was also placed with another inmate to ensure that he was accompanied at all times and that the authorities would be alerted to any sudden deterioration in his condition. The authorities also informed the Constitutional Court that the prison hospital had a 24-hour emergency service and that a fully equipped ambulance was available to the prison if it was ever needed.

96. As regards the second applicant, the Constitutional Court was informed that her blood pressure, pulse and weight were regularly checked by the prison doctor and that she was provided with vitamins. At the routine check carried out on 29 May 2017, the prison doctor had decided she should be transferred to the Cardiology Policlinic, which she had refused. The applicant had also refused to end her hunger strike despite being advised to do so by the prison doctor because of her deteriorating health condition.

97. On 28 June 2017 the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ application for an interim order. It held that their medical condition had been monitored from the moment they were put into detention and that they had refused attempts to transfer them to the prison hospital for further examination and treatment. Moreover, all precautions had been taken against any possible emergencies. In these circumstances, it was considered that there were no grounds to make an interim order, as it had not been shown that the applicants’ continued detention in the prison, where ongoing medical care was made available, would pose a risk to their lives or to their physical or mental integrity.
C. The Constitutional Court’s decision on the applicants’ substantive complaints
98. On 15 September 2021 the Constitutional Court delivered its judgment on the applicants’ complaints.

99. As regards the applicants’ complaints relating to their deprivation of liberty, the Constitutional Court observed at the outset that the order to detain them had concerned two offences – that is, membership of an armed terrorist organisation and acting in contravention of the Meeting and Demonstrations Act. The Constitutional Court stated, however, that it would examine the applicants’ complaint only in relation to the first of those offences, which was the one in relation to which the detention order had been carried out. No examination would be made in respect of the offence of violating the Meetings and Demonstrations Act, as that order had not been carried out and had therefore not resulted in any interference with the applicants’ liberty.

100. Turning to the merits of the applicants’ complaints, the Constitutional Court held that actions such as sit-ins or hunger strikes, which may under certain conditions be regarded as forms of the exercise of freedom of expression, should not, in themselves, be treated as criminal offences. It added, however, that such actions may be criminal where their execution is linked to terrorist activity, or where they involve conduct that amounts to praising, legitimising or encouraging the use of coercion, violence or threats by a terrorist organisation. The Constitutional Court found that, in the light of the evidence in the case file, the judicial authorities’ reliance on that evidence as a strong indication that the applicants had committed an offence linked to the DHKP/C could not be regarded as unfounded or arbitrary.

101. The Constitutional Court further held that the applicants’ pre-trial detention had pursued a legitimate aim and had been proportionate, given the nature of the offence against them. It considered that, in view of the severity of the penalty carried by the offence of membership of a terrorist organisation, there had been sufficient evidence of a risk of absconding or tampering with evidence. It therefore found that the decision that alternative judicial supervision measures would have been insufficient had not been unfounded, and declared the applicants’ complaints in that regard inadmissible.

102. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicants’ complaints relating to the violation of their right to life and physical integrity by reason of their detention despite their health condition, because the applicants had been released since making those complaints (see paragraphs 81 and 86 above). The Constitutional Court also found the applicants’ complaints that they had not had a fair hearing to be inadmissible, given that the criminal proceedings against them were still pending.
V. THE APPLICANTS’ REQUESTS TO THE COURT FOR AN INTERIM MEASURE
A. The applicants’ state of health prior to the lodging of an interim measure request with the Court

103. On 25 May 2017 the Ankara Medical Association, which had been monitoring the applicants’ state of health since the start of their hunger strike, lodged a request with the Central Prison Administration Division in the Ministry of Justice (Ceza ve Tevkifevleri Genel Müdürlüğü) to examine the applicants at the Sincan prison. On 29 May 2017 this request was rejected by the Central Prison Administration Division, which said that the examination and treatment of convicts and detainees was carried out in prison infirmaries or, where necessary, in State or university hospitals, under the relevant rules, and that there were no arrangements for examination and treatment outside the prison health system. Subsequent requests made to the Central Prison Administration or other authorities were rejected for similar reasons or left unanswered.

104. On 8 June 2017 the applicants’ lawyers asked the Ankara Medical Association to prepare an expert report on the applicants’ medical condition. Two reports were subsequently made, as described below, without any physical examination of the applicants.

105. The first report dated 14 June 2017 outlined the applicants’ condition up to their detention on the 75th day of their hunger strike. It stated that at that point the first and second applicants had lost 17 and 9 kilogrammes respectively. Both had experienced low blood pressure and a slow pulse rate, as well as infections resulting from weakened immune systems. The first applicant had also suffered from fatigue, headaches, memory problems and difficulty concentrating. The second applicant had had gastrointestinal problems and myopathy due to muscle protein breakdown, which had resulted in difficulty walking. The report stated that the health risks associated with the hunger strike had increased with the time subsequently spent in detention and had been further exacerbated by the conditions of that detention.

106. Referring in general to the weakened immune systems of persons on hunger strike, the report also listed certain measures necessary to preserve their health, such as the daily changing of clothes and bed linen, access to toilets and bathrooms which were cleaned daily, and maintaining an appropriate room temperature so as to prevent a loss of energy. Moreover, in view of their reduced strength and mobility, hunger strikers had to be accompanied and provided with suitable beds to prevent bedsores.

107. The second report was issued on 23 June 2017 by the Human Rights Committee of the Turkish Medical Association. This report provided general medical information on the effects of prolonged hunger strikes, which affected all bodily systems and organs and could lead to severe infections, permanent disorders, neurological problems, organ failure and death. The report stated that the extension of the detention and the lack of adequate medical monitoring would make intervention difficult in the event of life-threatening complications. The report also highlighted that only primary-level healthcare services were available in prisons. There was no access to specialised medical care, and the physical conditions were not compatible with the needs of persons on hunger strike. In terms of the applicants’ specific situations, the report observed – on the basis of the information obtained from the applicants’ lawyers during their visits – that although the applicants appeared to be taking their daily doses of vitamin B1, as well as fluids, sugar and salt, they were experiencing physical symptoms such as muscle weakness and pain, reduced mobility and gastrointestinal problems, as had also been observed in the Ankara Medical Association’s report (see paragraph 105 above). Moreover, since the start of the hunger strike, the first and second applicants had lost 22 and 18 kilogrammes respectively. The report concluded, against this background, that the applicants had reached a critical stage in their hunger strike and should therefore be released and undergo medical assessment by specialists.
B. The first interim measure request lodged with the Court

108. On 28 and 29 June 2017, respectively, the applicants lodged interim measure requests with the Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, seeking their release from detention in order to avoid a real risk of serious and irreparable harm, given that they had been on hunger strike since 9 March 2017.

109. On 30 June 2017 the Court decided to give notice of the applications to the respondent Government in accordance with Rule 40 of the Rules of Court. It invited them to provide information on the applicants’ state of health and to say whether their detention posed a risk to their life and whether they were being offered the necessary medical treatment, medical examination and medication in the prison. The Government were further invited to submit a detailed medical report by a panel of specialist doctors about the state of the applicants’ health, so that the Court could assess whether their detention in prison posed a threat to their life. The Court decided to suspend the examination of the interim measure request until it had received this information. Given the sensitive nature of the applications and the interests at stake, it also invited the applicants to call off their hunger strike and to cooperate with the prison doctors and medical staff to allow the necessary medical examinations to be carried out.
110. On 6 July 2017 the Government provided the Court with the following information, together with supporting documents:

- The applicants had undergone medical examinations by the prison doctor on admission to prison on 23 May 2017. They were warned of the risks of hunger striking and prescribed a daily intake of B1 (thiamine) and B12 vitamins, as well as specific doses of sugar, honey, salt, lemon, fruit, herbal tea and water. The prison doctor and health personnel checked the applicants’ blood sugar, blood pressure, pulse, temperature and weight four times a day.

- On 31 May 2017 the first applicant informed the prison authorities in writing that he would no longer consent to being treated by the prison doctor and would only accept treatment from the Ankara Medical Association. Thereafter he rejected the regular attempts by the prison doctor and health personnel to examine him. They nevertheless continued to monitor him daily. He was placed together with another inmate, to ensure that the prison administration would be informed of any sudden deterioration in his condition. A fully equipped ambulance was also made available for any emergencies.

- The second applicant did not refuse examination by the prison doctor in writing; however, it appears that shortly after being put into detention she likewise withdrew her consent to examination, except for being weighed once a week. She also refused a referral to the Cardiology Polyclinic despite her slow and irregular pulse (see paragraph 96 above).

- Subsequent attempts to transfer the applicants to the Sincan prison hospital and to have them examined by the Emergency Services and specialists from the prison hospital were similarly rejected. Nevertheless, in addition to the prison doctor and psychologist, the chief physician of the prison hospital, together with a number of specialists, continued to visit the applicants at regular intervals to observe their general state of health and to inform them of the potential harmful effects of being on hunger strike.

- On 29 and 30 June and 3 July 2017, that is, both prior to and following the Court’s invitation (see paragraph 109 above), the prison administration sought to refer the applicants to the Ankara Numune Hospital to determine whether their health was compatible with detention. The referral was rejected by both applicants, after consultation with their lawyers.

111. The Government contended that the national authorities were aware of the risk to the applicants’ health and lives and had taken the necessary measures to protect the applicants, but that they had failed to cooperate.

112. The applicants in turn informed the Court that they refused to be examined by the doctors provided by the prison administration as those doctors had reportedly expressed disapproval of their hunger strike and had referred to the possibility of “forced intervention” if they lost consciousness. The applicants therefore asked to be examined by independent specialist doctors.

113. On 10 July 2017 the Court asked the Government, inter alia, to immediately carry out a medical examination of the applicants in the presence of a doctor of their own choosing to determine whether detention was compatible with their state of health. It also repeated its request that the applicants call off their hunger strike and cooperate fully and immediately with the medical authorities.

114. In their response of 17 July 2017 the Government informed the Court that both applicants were examined at the prison hospital on 14 July 2017 by a committee of doctors consisting of the hospital’s chief physician and specialists in neurology, infectious diseases, internal medicine and emergency services, in the presence of a doctor of their own choosing, namely Dr Ş.K.F. The medical findings in respect of each applicant were recorded in a number of medical reports dated 17 July 2017 and signed by the above-mentioned medical committee (“the committee reports”).

115. The committee reports noted that both applicants were in moderate general condition, conscious, cooperative and oriented, but that their movements and responses were slowed and that they were suffering from muscle atrophy. The first applicant described experiencing occasional nausea and other gastrointestinal issues, as well as sores in his mouth and pain, tingling and cramp in his limbs. The second applicant also complained of gastrointestinal problems and occasional chest pain, as well as pain, tingling and cramp in her limbs, difficulty walking even with support, and intermittent short-term memory problems. The results of ECGs, chest scans and blood and urine tests showed low sodium levels, low uric acid levels and mild abnormality in liver function. An increased intake of vitamin K and salt was recommended to both applicants. Signs of impairment were noted in both applicants’ peripheral nervous system and the first applicant also suffered from problems with her vestibular system. The committee observed that while the first applicant showed no signs of encephalopathy, the second applicant ran a risk of developing Wernicke’s encephalopathy due to thiamine deficiency if the hunger strike continued.
