It was also concluded that, given the risk of irreparable harm to their health, both applicants should be referred to the Medical Board of the Numune Hospital for a conclusive assessment of their fitness to remain in detention.

116. On 17 July 2017 Dr Ş.K.F., who had not yet at that point received the medical committee’s report referred to in paragraph 115 above, prepared separate reports setting out her observations in respect of each applicant. Dr Ş.K.F.’s findings on the applicants’ medical conditions largely corresponded with those in the committee reports. Dr Ş.K.F. emphasised that both applicants were experiencing difficulties in moving and meeting their basic needs, and therefore required assistance. In this connection, the first applicant complained of difficulties because his place of detention was over two floors. He said that although the authorities had moved his bed to the lower floor, where the toilet was located, to facilitate his access to it, they had not moved his cupboard, and that he had difficulty using the squat toilet. The second applicant complained that her cell was cold, lacked sufficient sunlight and that there were ants in her cell. She also complained that the tap water looked dirty, raising concerns about hygiene and the risk of infection.

117. Given the applicants’ continued refusal to undergo medical examination by doctors other than those of their own choosing, Dr Ş.K.F. expressed concern that any metabolic or other complications that might arise could not be addressed promptly, and that depriving the applicants of their liberty could therefore in itself pose a risk to their lives. She therefore advised that the applicants’ medical condition required their release from detention and their monitoring in a civilian medical facility.

118. In the meantime, between 12 and 18 July 2017, a series of measures were taken to improve the physical conditions of the first applicant’s detention by accommodating his physical needs arising from his loss of muscle mass. The squat toilet in his detention unit was replaced with a sitting toilet, and he was provided with a medical air mattress as well as a cupboard near his bed. A wheelchair was assigned for his use outside the detention unit and access ramps were installed so that he could use the wheelchair when leaving the room – although he described to the Court an incident in which he had not been allowed to seek assistance from his cellmate in using the wheelchair.

119. On 21 July 2017 the Government informed the Court that both applicants were refusing to undergo further medical examination at the Numune Hospital in keeping with the recommendation in the committee reports (see paragraph 115 above), even in the presence of a doctor of their choice.
120. On 21 July 2017 the Court urged the applicants, once again, to cooperate with the national authorities.

121. In a letter sent on the same day, the applicants’ lawyer submitted that, in view of their fragile condition, subjecting the applicants to further medical examinations at the Numune Hospital would impose a disproportionate burden on them and would place their lives at risk. He also argued that the medical reports drawn up by doctors at the prison hospital (see paragraph 115 above) was sufficient for the purposes of the request under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, a view that was shared by Dr Ş.F.K. That being said, following the Court’s call for the applicants to cooperate with the national authorities, they had reconsidered their position and had agreed to be examined at Numune Hospital.

122. Accordingly, on 25 July 2017 the applicants were transferred to the Numune Hospital by ambulance. At the hospital, they were examined by ten specialists, none of whom were members of the Medical Board that would determine the applicants’ fitness to remain in detention (see paragraph 115 above). The examinations were conducted in the presence of their doctor of choice, Dr. Ş.F.K. The applicants’ lawyer reported that the applicants were met with hundreds of police officers and gendarmes at the hospital, and the examinations were conducted in a basement room which was allegedly unfit for carrying out a medical examination, and which lacked sufficient ventilation and light. He also said that the transfer conditions to and from the hospital, as well as the security personnel’s handling of the applicants, had been very harsh.
123. After the examination, the applicants were asked to return to the Numune Hospital on 27 July 2017 for further examination, including by members of the above-mentioned Board.

124. On 27 July 2017 the applicants refused to be taken to the Numune Hospital for further examination in order to avoid being subjected to the same harsh conditions that they had allegedly experienced on 25 July 2017 (see paragraph 122 above). On the same date, the applicant’s doctor, Dr Ş.F.K., confirmed in a report the allegedly adverse conditions under which the applicants had been examined on 25 July 2017. She also reported that the examination conducted on that day had been unnecessary, given that all necessary information on the applicants’ health status had already been obtained during the examinations at the prison hospital, which had been comprehensive and sufficient (see paragraphs 114-115 above).

125. On the night of 27 July 2017, three doctors from the Numune Hospital went to the prison complex where the applicants were being held in order to examine them. The second applicant was taken to the prison infirmary at 11.05 p.m. to meet the doctors but refused to be examined. She explained to the doctors that the transfer to the hospital on 25 July 2017 and the ensuing examinations had been extremely arduous for her, that she had nearly fainted from fatigue, and that she would not be able to tolerate another transfer and another round of examinations. The doctors subsequently visited the first applicant sometime between 11.30 p.m. and 11.50 p.m. He refused to be examined except in the presence of his doctor.

126. On 28 July 2017 the Medical Board of the Numune Hospital issued medical reports based on the examinations conducted on 25 July 2017 (see paragraph 122 above), which found that the applicants’ condition was life‑threatening and they were no longer able to live without assistance. The reports nevertheless concluded as follows:

“[T]hese findings do not require the pre-trial detention to be suspended. [The applicants’] condition can be monitored and [they] can be treated in prisons equipped with medical facilities comparable to those of a hospital or in sections of public health institutions designated for detainees.”
127. The Government said that the applicants did not object to this report and did not ask for the available reports to be reevaluated by the Forensic Medicine Institute.

128. After receiving the above-mentioned reports from the Numune Hospital, at around midnight on 28 July 2017, the prison authorities informed the applicants that it had been decided that they would be admitted to the Sincan prison hospital. The records provided by the Government showed that the applicants were also informed in writing that they could continue their hunger strike at the hospital if they so wished. Following their refusal, the applicants were forcibly removed from their rooms on stretchers and transferred to the prison hospital by ambulance.

129. On 31 July 2017 the applicants’ representative contacted the Court about the applicants’ transfer from the Sincan prison to the Sincan prison hospital. He claimed first of all that the conditions in which the transfer had taken place, particularly in respect of the first applicant, had been unacceptable, as he was tied to the stretcher for showing resistance and had travelled to the prison hospital in an ambulance in that position, causing bruises and lesions. During a visit to the applicants at the Sincan prison hospital on 29 July 2017, two of the applicant’s lawyers in the domestic proceedings, including Mr D.E. Aydın, who is currently representing him before the Court (see paragraph 2 above), brought those matters to the attention of the doctors at the hospital. They were told in response to take any complaints to the public prosecutor’s office.

130. The representative claimed secondly that despite the clear indication in the Medical Board’s report that the applicants needed constant assistance (see paragraph 126 above), they had not been provided with any assistance since their transfer to the hospital, as a result of which they were experiencing difficulties in meeting their most basic needs.

131. The representative stated lastly that the lawyers who visited the applicants at the prison hospital had noted that the physical conditions in the hospital room were harsher than in the prison, where they had enjoyed access to an independent courtyard.

132. On 2 August 2017 the Court rejected the applicants’ requests for an interim measure requiring their immediate release. Having reviewed the requests in the light of the medical reports and other information provided by the parties, it found that their detention at the Sincan prison hospital did not pose a real and imminent risk of irreparable harm to their lives or their health. It further informed the parties that it expected the Government to take all necessary measures to ensure that the applicants’ rights under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention were respected, including ensuring that appropriate arrangements were made to assist them with their daily needs, given the Numune Hospital’s report that they were unable to live without assistance (see paragraph 126 above). It also asked the Government to allow the applicants to consult doctors of their own choosing at the prison hospital, should they so wish, in order to enable them to decide whether to continue their hunger strike. The Court lastly called on the applicants to end their hunger strike.
C. The applicants’ detention at Sincan Prison Hospital
133. As explained in paragraph 128 above, on 28 July 2017 the applicants were transferred from Sincan prison to the State hospital within the prison complex.

134. On 18 August 2017 the Government provided information as to the treatment and care received by the applicants at the prison hospital, as well as about the conditions in which they were held. The Government submitted that the applicants were under constant monitoring by the hospital’s palliative care service, with arrangements in place for any emergencies. A care and treatment plan was established, including regular monitoring of their vital signs, consultations with specialist doctors and a psychiatrist, and the prescription of vitamins and other medication. However, the applicants declined most of the treatment, accepting only certain vitamins and fluids. The Government provided the Court with the prison hospital medical team’s daily records of their visits to the applicants’ rooms, during which the risks of the hunger strike were explained, and the applicants were offered medical examinations and treatment, and their refusals were recorded. It appears from the information and documents submitted to the Court that a panel of specialists from the Numune Hospital also visited the applicants daily to assess their health, inform them of their condition and warn them of the risks they faced as a result of the hunger strike. The applicants and their families were also informed on several occasions that the law allowed for intervention if it was necessary once a critical stage was reached in the applicants’ conditions.

135. To prevent the risk of infection, anyone entering the applicants’ rooms wore masks and gloves, and hand sanitisers were also made available in the rooms. The applicants were visited by a nurse at very frequent intervals and their rooms were cleaned daily. Initially, the nurse’s visits were scheduled for every hour. However, on 4 August 2017 the first applicant was recorded as having said he was disturbed by these hourly visits and stated that it was because of those visits that his request to be accompanied by a family member was not being granted. The first applicant was subsequently informed that he could lodge a petition to be accompanied by a family member (see paragraph 138 et. seq. below).

136. Moreover, in accordance with the Court’s letter of 2 August 2017 (see paragraph 132 above), the authorities had asked the applicants to give the names of three doctors that they might wish to consult with a view to making a decision as to whether or not to call off their hunger strike. When the applicants provided their list on 14 August 2017, the Ankara principal public prosecutor’s office had authorised the named doctors to be admitted to the prison hospital and to have access to the applicants in the presence of the prison hospital doctors. On 15 August 2017, both applicants refused to undergo examination by a panel composed of their doctors of choice together with doctors from the prison hospital and the Numune Hospital, asking instead to be examined exclusively by their own doctors. On this occasion, the applicants were once again informed of the possible consequences and risks of their prolonged hunger strike.

137. As for the material conditions of the applicants’ detention, the Government described that they were held in rooms measuring 330 cm by 350 cm and equipped with an LCD TV, mini refrigerator, locker, dining table and chair, a cabinet and a separate bathroom arranged for use of disabled persons. The rooms received sufficient light through a window measuring 195 cm by 146 cm and were cleaned and disinfected at least once a day. The bedspread and sheets were changed regularly. The applicants were also provided with medical air mattresses to prevent bedsores. In support of their arguments, the Government provided photographs of the rooms where the applicants were held at the prison hospital. They also provided a report issued by that hospital, dated 7 August 2017, attesting to those conditions.

138. Furthermore, arrangements had been made to ensure that the applicants were “accompanied” at the prison hospital, as indicated in the Medical Board’s report of 28 July 2017 (see paragraph 126 above). A meeting was held on 31 July 2017 under the supervision of the Ankara chief public prosecutor’s office, where it was decided that the applicants’ need for companions could be met by public servants, given the “sensitivity of their situation”. It appears from the information provided by the Government that members of the hospital’s “procurement personnel” were initially assigned as patient caregivers to assist the applicants with their personal care and needs, in the company of health personnel. However, the applicants refused to have their personal care and needs met in this manner and brought their grievances in this regard to the attention of the authorities. The Government provided that a medical officer and a “guardian” nevertheless visited the applicants regularly for their personal needs.

139. It appears from the hospital records provided by the Government that following their visit of the applicants on 7 August 2017, the panel of specialists from the Numune Hospital (see paragraph 134 above) reported that, given their circumstances, it would be appropriate for the applicants to be accompanied at the hospital by an immediate family member. On 10 August 2017 the applicants therefore asked to be accompanied by their mother and sister respectively. This request was granted by the Ankara public prosecutor’s office with effect from 15 August 2017. From that date onwards, the applicants were accompanied at the prison hospital on a 24-hour basis.

140. It further appears from the information in the case file that on 26 September 2017 the second applicant was transferred to the ICU at the Numune Hospital for monitoring (see paragraph 141 et. seq.). Five doctors from the prison hospital had signed a report earlier that day saying that the second applicant’s transfer to the ICU was considered necessary in the light of the deterioration in her medical condition, as evidenced by her reduced oral intake, impaired sense of taste, and increased drowsiness, as well as the absence of any medical tests or vital measurements since 29 July 2017.
D. The second interim measure request lodged with the Court

141. On 29 September 2017 the applicants’ lawyer repeated the request to the Court for it to indicate an interim measure for the applicants’ release under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, in view of the growing threat posed to their lives and physical integrity because of their detention. He pointed in particular to the significant deterioration in the conditions of the second applicant’s detention following her transfer from the prison hospital to the ICU at the Numune Hospital, against her will (see paragraphs 66 and 76 above).

142. He submitted in this connection that the transfer had taken place on 26 September 2017 at 2.00 a.m. No explanation was given to either the second applicant or her lawyers as to why the transfer was medically necessary. In fact, the medical report drawn up on her admission to the ICU indicated that the applicant was “breathing spontaneously, conscious, cooperative, and oriented, respond[ing] logically to questions, and express[ing] her needs” but that she continued to refuse treatment and medical examination. Reportedly, she was informed that her discharge from the ICU would not be authorised unless she consented to a blood test to measure her blood values, which she did not. Since there did not appear to be any documented deterioration in the second applicant’s medical condition, the lawyer argued that the decision to transfer her to the ICU had been motivated by non-medical reasons.

143. The lawyer further argued that one of the second applicant’s lawyers had briefly visited her at the hospital, enabling first-hand observation of her material conditions of detention, particularly the lack of appropriate sanitary facilities (see also paragraphs 66, 76 and 141 above). It was noted in this connection that there was no toilet available to the applicant; she was asked to use a commode chair next to her bed to meet her toileting needs. She would have had to place a plastic bag in the hole in the commode, which she was unable to do. Moreover, she had no means of cleaning herself afterwards, was deprived of the assistance that she had been permitted at the prison hospital, and had no privacy, since gendarmerie officers maintained constant surveillance. He further submitted that the gendarmerie officers did not allow her to leave the bed and had threatened to handcuff her to the bed by her arms and legs if she attempted to get up.

144. In a further letter submitted on 2 October 2017, the lawyer asserted that despite the Court’s indication in its decision of 2 August 2017 (see paragraph 132 above), the second applicant was not allowed to consult with a doctor of her choice. In this connection, although a request for such consultation was authorised by the Ministry of Health on 29 September 2017, the doctor was denied access by the police stationed outside the ICU.

145. On 3 October 2017 the Court decided not to indicate to the respondent Government the interim measure sought by the applicants. However, having regard to the allegations made as regards in particular the deterioration in the second applicant’s conditions of detention, the Court nevertheless asked the Government to ensure that adequate measures were taken to assist the applicants with their daily needs, including, if they so wished, consultations with doctors of their choice, so as to enable them to decide whether or not to continue their hunger strike.
VI. SUBSEQUENT DEVELOPMENTS

146. On 5 October 2017 a doctor from the Ankara Medical Association was authorised to visit and examine the second applicant. The report prepared by this doctor reiterated that no medical justification had been given for keeping the second applicant at the ICU and also corroborated the observations previously made to the Court as regards the material conditions of her detention (see paragraph 143 above). The doctor also reported that the second applicant was not able to take showers while in the ICU and that she had therefore not been able to wash herself since her transfer there on 26 September 2017, which increased the risk of infection. Nor was she provided with clean clothes, although a daily change of clothes was required for persons on hunger strike. Moreover, because she was deprived of assistance in the ICU, the second applicant faced difficulties in preparing and noting her daily intake of drinks, vitamins, sugar and salt. The report further confirmed that the gendarmerie officers did not allow the applicant to move around the room, which meant she was confined to her bed at all times. It also stated that the applicant was living under the constant fear of force-feeding in the ICU, which caused her considerable psychological stress.

147. On 9 October 2017 the second applicant was discharged from the ICU and taken to the prison ward of the Numune Hospital. She claimed that the material conditions there were similarly incompatible with her health condition and with the requirements of Article 3 (see paragraph 201 below for further details).

148. The second applicant was discharged from the prison ward of the Numune Hospital on 1 December 2017, following her conviction by the trial court and the order for her release (see paragraphs 85 and 86 above).

149. Both applicants ended their hunger strike on 26 January 2018, following the rejection of their objection to their dismissal by the ad hoc Commission established for the examination of measures taken under the state of emergency (see Köksal v. Turkey (dec.), no. 70478/16, §§ 16 and 25, 6 June 2017).
VII. JOINT URGENT APPEAL BY THE WORKING GROUP ON ARBITRARY DETENTION

150. On 1 June 2017 the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (the “WGAD”) sent a letter to the Government of Türkiye about the detention and hunger strike of the applicants and three others, including the mother and the wife of the first applicant. The letter, which was a joint urgent appeal signed by the Vice-Chair of the WGAD and five UN Special Rapporteurs, and which invited the Government to submit observations on, inter alia, the applicants’ detention and the health care provided to them, concluded as follows:

“We would like to inform your Excellency’s Government that after having transmitted an urgent appeal to the Government, the Working Group on Arbitrary Detention may transmit the case through its regular procedure in order to render an opinion on whether the deprivation of liberty was arbitrary or not. Such urgent appeals in no way prejudge any opinion the Working Group may render. The Government is required to respond separately for the urgent appeal procedure and the regular procedure.”
151. On an unspecified date, the Government submitted the observations requested to the WGAD.
152. There is no information in the case file to suggest that the WGAD has subsequently taken up the case through its regular procedure to render an opinion.
RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE
DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
A. Domestic law relating to the charges brought against the applicants
153. Article 314 of the CC (Law no. 5237 of 26 September 2004) provides as follows:

“(1) Anyone who forms or leads an armed organisation with the purpose of committing the offences listed in the fourth and fifth parts of this chapter shall be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of ten to fifteen years.
(2) Any member of an organisation referred to in the first paragraph shall be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of five to ten years.”
154. Section 7 (2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713 of 12 April 1991) reads as follows:

“Anyone who disseminates propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation by legitimising or condoning methods used by such organisations entailing coercion, violence or threats or incites others to use such methods shall be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of one to five years. ...”
155. The relevant provisions of the Meetings and Demonstrations Act (Law no. 2911) read:
Prohibition of incitement

“It is prohibited to encourage or incite the public to participate in an unlawful meeting or demonstration by addressing the public directly, by speaking or making announcements through any sound-amplifying or sound-transmitting device or instrument, by posting or distributing printed, reproduced, handwritten or hand-drawn papers on walls or elsewhere, or by similar means and methods.

“Persons taking part in unlawful meetings or demonstrations who continue not to disperse despite warnings or use of force shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between six months and three years. If the offender is one of the organisers of the meeting or the demonstration, the sentence to be imposed pursuant to this paragraph shall be increased by half.
Instigators and accomplices

“Unless the act constitutes a separate offence carrying a heavier penalty, anyone who acts in contravention of the prohibition in section 27 shall be sentenced to imprisonment for a term of one year and six months to four years, provided that the meeting or procession either did not take place or, having taken place, was dispersed following the first order and warning; where the meeting or demonstration is dispersed by force, the penalty shall be imprisonment for a term of three to five years.”
B. Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP)
156. Pre-trial detention is governed by Article 100 et. seq. of the CCP. The relevant parts of Article 100 §§ 1 and 2, which relate to the grounds for detention, provide as follows:

“1. Where there is specific evidence giving rise to a strong suspicion of an offence and grounds for detention, a detention order may be made in respect of the suspect or accused. However, no detention order may be made where it would be disproportionate to the importance of the case or to the expected sentence or preventive measure.
2. In the cases specified below, grounds for detention may be deemed to exist:
(a) if there are specific facts giving rise to a finding of [a risk of] absconding ...;
(b) if the conduct of the suspect or accused gives rise to a strong suspicion
(1) that evidence might be destroyed, concealed or tampered with;
(2) that there might be an attempt to put pressure on witnesses, victims or other individuals ...”
For certain offences listed in Article 100 § 3 of the CCP, there is a statutory presumption of grounds for detention. Article 100 § 3 of the CCP provided as follows at the material time:
“3. If there are facts giving rise to a strong suspicion that [any of] the offences listed below have been committed, it can be presumed that there are grounds for detention:
(a) for the following crimes provided for in the Criminal Code (no. 5237 of 26 September 2004):
(11) crimes against the constitutional order and against the functioning of the constitutional system (Articles 309, 310, 311, 312, 313, 314, 315);
157. Article 101 of the CCP, which governs orders for pre-trial detention, provided as follows at the material time:

“1. During the investigation stage, a decision to detain the suspect shall be taken by the magistrate at the request of the public prosecutor; during the trial stage, a decision to detain the accused shall be taken by the court, either at the request of the public prosecutor or of its own motion. Such requests must be reasoned and must set out the legal and factual grounds demonstrating that the application of judicial supervision measures would be insufficient.
2. In decisions ordering detention, extending detention, or rejecting a request for release, the evidence demonstrating:
(a) the strong suspicion of an offence;
(b) the existence of grounds for detention; and
(c) the proportionality of the detention measure,
shall be clearly demonstrated and substantiated by specific facts...”

158. Under Article 109 of the CCP, even if all the grounds for detention were present, the court had the option of placing a suspect under judicial supervision instead of ordering detention. Paragraph 3 of that provision provides as follows:
" 3. Judicial supervision involves the imposition on the suspect of one or more of the following obligations:
(b) To report regularly, within the specified periods, to the places designated by the judge.
(j) Not to leave his residence.
C. Law no. 5275 on the enforcement of sentences and preventive measures
159. Section 82 (2) of this Law reads as follows:

“Where convicted persons refuse nourishment and engage in a hunger strike or a death fast, and where, despite the measures taken and efforts made pursuant to paragraph 1, a physician determines that they have entered a life-threatening condition or that their consciousness is impaired, medical measures such as examination, diagnostic procedures, treatment and feeding shall be carried out, irrespective of their wishes, within the [prison] or, where this is not possible, by immediate transfer to a hospital, provided that such measures do not pose a risk to their health or life.”
D. Regulation of 20 March 2006 on the management of prisons and the execution of sentences and preventive measures, published in the Official Gazette of 6 April 2006 (repealed on 29 March 2020)
160. The relevant provisions of this Regulation concerning the medical treatment of convicted persons outside prison, as in force at the material time, were as follows:

“1. A convicted person shall have the right to benefit from medical examination and treatment facilities, as well as medical equipment, for the protection of his or her physical and mental health and for the diagnosis of illnesses. For this purpose, the convicted person shall first be treated in the [prison] infirmary; where this is not possible, he or she shall be treated in the prison wards of a State or university hospital.”

3. Where convicted persons receive inpatient treatment outside the [prison], their spouse, mother, father, sibling or child—or, in their absence, another relative deemed appropriate by the chief public prosecutor’s office—may be allowed to stay with them as an accompanying person, provided that this is confirmed to be necessary in a report by the treating physician.”
By virtue of section 186, those provisions also applied to persons detained on remand.
E. Report of the National Human Rights Institution of Türkiye on the conditions on the prison ward of the Numune Hospital

161. On 16 April 2015 the National Human Rights Institution of Türkiye reported on the conditions on the prison ward of the Numune Hospital, where the second applicant was held between 9 October and 1 December 2017.

162. The report described the prison ward as located in the basement of the hospital and consisting of four rooms, each containing five beds and secured by iron doors. Ventilation and lighting in the rooms were reported to be highly inadequate; patients had no access to daylight or fresh air. The rooms were illuminated not by natural light but by artificial lighting, the control of which rested with prison officers, one of the lights remaining permanently switched on.

163. Patients were reportedly unable to change their clothes or obtain fresh clothing, and no facilities were provided for washing garments. No bathing facilities were available, and essential personal hygiene items were either unavailable or difficult to obtain.
II. INTERNATIONAL MATERIAL
A. Secretary General of the Council of Europe

164. During the plenary session of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe held on 26 June 2017, a number of parliamentarians raised concerns regarding the mass dismissal of civil servants in Türkiye by emergency legislative decrees following the attempted coup, and inquired as to the steps taken by the Council of Europe with regard to the specific situation of the present applicants. In his response to the Assembly, the then Secretary General of the Council of Europe called for the release of the applicants and said that he would also raise this call directly with the relevant Turkish authorities[2].

165. In a further press release issued on 20 July 2017, the then Secretary General of the Council of Europe reiterated his concerns over the situation of the applicants and repeated his call for their release[3]. He also appealed to the applicants to stop their hunger strike.
B. Committee of Ministers

166. Recommendation No. R (98) 7 of the Committee of Ministers to member States concerning the ethical and organisational aspects of health care in prison (adopted by the Committee of Ministers on 8 April 1998 at the 627th meeting of the Ministers’ Deputies) provides as follows, as relevant:
“C. Patient’s consent and confidentiality
17. Remand prisoners should be entitled to ask for a consultation with their own doctor or another outside doctor at their own expense.
E. Refusal of treatment, hunger strike

60. In the case of refusal of treatment, the doctor should request a written statement signed by the patient in the presence of a witness. The doctor should give the patient full information as to the likely benefits of medication, possible therapeutic alternatives, and warn him/her about risks associated with his/her refusal. It should be ensured that the patient has a full understanding of his/her situation...

61. The clinical assessment of a hunger striker should be carried out only with the express permission of the patient, unless he or she suffers from serious mental disorders which require the transfer to a psychiatric service.
62. Hunger strikers should be given an objective explanation of the harmful effects of their action upon their physical well-being, so that they understand the dangers of prolonged hunger striking.

63. If, in the opinion of the doctor, the hunger striker’s condition is becoming significantly worse, it is essential that the doctor report this fact to the appropriate authority and take action in accordance with national legislation (including professional standards).”

167. The Recommendation of the Committee of Ministers to member States of the Council of Europe on the European Prison Rules (Rec (2006)2), adopted on 11 January 2006 at the 952nd meeting of the Ministers’ Deputies, as revised in 2020, in so far as relevant, reads as follows:
“18.2 In all buildings where prisoners are required to live, work or congregate:

a. the windows shall be large enough to enable the prisoners to read or work by natural light in normal conditions and shall allow the entrance of fresh air except where there is an adequate air conditioning system;
19.3 Prisoners shall have ready access to sanitary facilities that are hygienic and respect privacy.

19.4 Adequate facilities shall be provided so that every prisoner may have a bath or shower, at a temperature suitable to the climate, if possible daily but at least twice a week (or more frequently if necessary) in the interest of general hygiene.
27.1 Every prisoner shall be provided with the opportunity of at least one hour of exercise every day in the open air, if the weather permits.”
C. European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“the CPT”)
168. The relevant extracts from the CPT Standards of “Health care services in prisons” [CPT/Inf/E (2002) 1, Rev. 2011] and from the 3rd General Report [CPT/Inf (93) 12] read as follows:
“c. Patient’s consent and confidentiality

In the event of a hunger strike, public authorities or professional organisations in some countries will require the doctor to intervene to prevent death as soon as the patient’s consciousness becomes seriously impaired. In other countries, the rule is to leave clinical decisions to the doctor in charge, after he has sought advice and weighed up all the relevant facts.
d. Preventive health care

53. It lies with prison health care services - as appropriate acting in conjunction with other authorities - to supervise ... conditions of hygiene (cleanliness of clothing and bedding; access to running water; sanitary installations) as well as the heating, lighting and ventilation of cells. Work and outdoor exercise arrangements should also be taken into consideration.”
169. An extract from the 26th General Report of the CPT on remand detention (CPT/Inf(2017)5-part) provides as follows, as relevant:

In this regard, the CPT considers that all detained persons, irrespective of their legal status and the place in which they are being held, should have effective access to medical services. Further, remand prisoners should in principle be given the opportunity to consult and be treated by their own doctor (it being understood that this may be carried out at their own expense).”

170. An extract from the 30th General Report of the CPT on a decency threshold for prisons – criteria for assessing conditions of detention (CPT/Inf(2021)5-part) – provides as follows, as relevant (footnotes omitted):
“68. The Committee considers that all persons deprived of their liberty in prisons should be provided, at minimum, with:
- decent sleeping and living conditions and the means to keep clean: proper sanitation, including toilet and shower facilities, washing water, cleaning products, laundry, personal hygiene products;
72. ... [A]ll prisoners must ... benefit from heating, artificial and natural light, ventilation and access to fresh air, as well as from sufficient personal living space.

73. To reach a decency threshold, all prisoners must also be provided with the means to keep themselves clean, including ready access to a clean fully-functioning toilet, proper sanitation, warm washing water, shower (if possible on a daily basis, but at least twice a week), cleaning products, laundry facilities and personal hygiene products.
74... Prisoners should be supplied with, or allowed to retain, a sufficient amount of clothing.
80. The CPT has repeatedly emphasised that all prisoners must benefit from a minimum of access to one hour’s daily outdoor exercise and/or time in the open air, ...”
JOINDER OF THE APPLICATIONS
171. Having regard to the similar subject matter of the applications, the Court finds it appropriate to examine them jointly in a single judgment.

172. As will be described in detail below, the applicants complained in their present applications that their pre-trial detention was incompatible with Articles 2 and 3 and Article 5 §§ 1, 3 and 4 of the Convention (see paragraphs 195, 256 and 307 below). These complaints were communicated to the Government on 2 October 2017.

173. After this notification, the second applicant made new submissions concerning the factual developments in the case. These were mainly about the conditions of her detention at the prison ward of the Numune Hospital, where she was transferred on 9 October 2017; they are summarised in paragraph 147 above and 201 below. The Court reiterates that, as a general rule, it does not examine any new matters raised after the communication of the application, unless the new matters are an elaboration of the applicant’s original complaints to the Court (see Ilgar Mammadov v. Azerbaijan, no. 15172/13, § 78, 22 May 2014). The Court notes that the second applicant’s original application involved complaints relating to the incompatibility of her detention, including the material conditions in which she was held, with her state of health. Her subsequent submissions regarding the conditions at the prison ward of the Numune Hospital therefore did not constitute a new matter but concerned the factual developments in the proceedings relating to the applicant’s continued detention in the framework of the same proceedings. They therefore fall within the scope of the present case (see, mutatis mutandis, Aliyev v. Azerbaijan, nos. 68762/14 and 71200/14, §§ 93-95, 20 September 2018). In any event, the Government were provided with the opportunity to comment on the second applicant’s submissions in this regard.

174. The Court further observes that in their subsequent submissions both applicants also raised a number of additional issues relating to their right to defence, the right to appear before a judge and the right to be presumed innocent. The Court finds that those issues constitute new complaints and not an elaboration or elucidation of the applicants’ original complaints to the Court which were communicated to the Government (see, mutatis mutandis, Radomilja and Others v. Croatia [GC], nos. 37685/10 and 22768/12, §§ 122 and 128-36, 20 March 2018). There is, moreover, no information to show that the applicants complied with the admissibility requirements in Article 35 § 1 of the Convention in relation to those new issues raised (ibid., § 135; see also Fu Quan, s.r.o. v. the Czech Republic [GC], no. 24827/14, § 147, 1 June 2023). Those issues therefore fall outside the scope of the present case and will not be taken into consideration (see, for instance, Kulák v. Slovakia, no. 57748/21, § 52, 3 April 2025, and Alakhverdyan v. Ukraine, no. 8838/20, § 43, 26 June 2025).
III. PRELIMINARY QUESTION CONCERNING THE DEROGATION BY TÜRKİYE

175. The Government asserted that the applicants’ complaints under Article 5 of the Convention should be examined with due regard to the derogation by Türkiye of which the Secretary General of the Council of Europe had been notified on 21 July 2016 under Article 15 of the Convention (see paragraph 6 above; for the full text of the notice of derogation, see Yüksel Yalçınkaya v. Türkiye [GC], no. 15669/20, § 205, 26 September 2023). They argued in particular that “the use of detention as a measure was inevitable in the existing situation in Türkiye”, given the threat posed to the life of the nation by the attempted military coup and other terrorist acts that followed it.
176. The applicants contested the Government’s request.

177. In its judgment in Mehmet Hasan Altan v. Turkey (no. 13237/17, § 93, 20 March 2018), the Court held that the attempted military coup had indeed disclosed the existence of a “public emergency threatening the life of the nation” within the meaning of the Convention. As to whether the measures taken in the present case were strictly required by the exigencies of the situation and consistent with the other obligations under international law, these points will be considered as part of the examination of the relevant complaints on the merits (see paragraph 305 below; see also Yüksel Yalçınkaya, cited above, § 213, and Tuğluk v. Türkiye, no. 71757/17, § 64, 14 October 2025).
IV. THE GOVERNMENT’S PRELIMINARY OBJECTIONS
A. Preliminary objection under Article 35 § 2 (b) of the Convention

178. The Government argued that the applicants had submitted their complaints to another procedure of international investigation or settlement within the meaning of Article 35 § 2 (b) of the Convention, namely the WGAD (see paragraphs 150-152 above), and invited the Court to dismiss the applications as being inadmissible on that ground.

179. The applicants contested the Government’s argument and stated that they had never lodged an application with the WGAD, or any other international body. The WGAD had initiated action regarding their situation of its own motion, and had only sought their consent to disclose their names in the urgent appeal described in paragraph 150 above.

180. The Court has previously examined the WGAD process and concluded that this Working Group was indeed a “procedure of international investigation or settlement” within the meaning of Article 35 § 2 (b) of the Convention (see Peraldi v. France (dec.), no. 2096/05, 7 April 2009, and Sabuncu and Others v. Turkey, no. 23199/17, § 112, 10 November 2020; for the “urgent action” procedure of the WGAD see also Kavala v. Turkey, no. 28749/18, §§ 78-79, 10 December 2019).

181. As observed in the letter referred to in paragraph 150 above, an urgent appeal may give rise to the opening of a regular procedure, in the context of which the WGAD is called upon to issue an opinion as to whether or not an instance of deprivation of liberty was arbitrary. An opinion issued under the WGAD’s regular procedure, involving the same parties and relating to the same facts and complaints as in an application before the Court, may indeed lead to the application being declared inadmissible under Article 35 § 2 (b) of the Convention (see, for instance, Peraldi, cited above, and M.J. v. Azerbaijan (dec.), no. 19657/18, §§ 9-13, 22 February 2024), unlike in the case of an urgent appeal that does not culminate in the adoption of such an opinion (see Kavala, cited above, § 93). There is nothing in the case file to suggest that a regular procedure was opened before the WGAD or that an opinion was issued in respect of the present applicants (see paragraph 152 above). The Court further observes that the applicants’ allegation that they never made an application to the WGAD (see paragraph 179 above) has not been contested by the Government.
182. The Government’s objection under Article 35 § 2 (b) of the Convention must accordingly be dismissed.
B. Preliminary objection of non-exhaustion of domestic remedies
1. The parties’ submissions

183. The Government raised a number of objections regarding non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. They argued firstly that the applicants should have lodged a domestic compensation claim pursuant to Article 141 of the CCP in respect of their complaints under Article 5 of the Convention.

184. The Government secondly claimed that the applicants had failed to bring an action for a full remedy (tam yargı davası) in the administrative courts under Article 125 of the Constitution and section 2 of the Administrative Procedure Act (Law no. 2577), which would have enabled them to seek compensation in respect of the allegedly wrongful administrative actions they had been subjected to.

185. The Government lastly argued that at the time of the lodging of the present applications with the Court, the proceedings commenced by the applicants in the Constitutional Court were still pending.

186. The applicants contested the Government’s arguments and maintained that they had exhausted all available and effective domestic remedies. They claimed in particular that a compensation claim could not have led to an acknowledgment that they had been deprived of their liberty unlawfully in contravention of the guarantees under Article 5 §§ 1 (c) and 3 of the Convention.
2. The Court’s assessment

187. The Court reiterates at the outset the general principles developed in its case-law regarding the rule of exhaustion of domestic remedies under Article 35 § 1 of the Convention (see, for instance, Vučković and Others v. Serbia (preliminary objection) [GC], nos. 17153/11 and 29 others, §§ 69‑77, 25 March 2014, and Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS) v. Switzerland [GC], no. 21881/20, §§ 138-144, 27 November 2023).

188. Turning first to the Government’s argument regarding the applicants’ failure to exhaust the remedy provided under Article 141 of the CCP in respect of their complaints under Article 5 of the Convention (see paragraph 183 above), the Court notes that similar arguments raised by the Government have already been dismissed in other cases against Türkiye (see, for instance, Selahattin Demirtaş v. Turkey (no. 2) [GC], no. 14305/17, §§ 205-214, 22 December 2020; Kocamış and Kurt v. Turkey, no. 227/13, § 39, 25 January 2022; and Tuğluk v. Türkiye, no. 71757/17, §§ 76-79, 14 October 2025). In this connection, the Court has held that a compensation claim under Article 141 of the CCP could not be regarded as an effective remedy for complaints raised under Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention (see, for instance, Selahattin Demirtaş, cited above, § 214, and Tuğluk, cited above, § 78). It has also held, in so far as the complaints under Article 5 § 4 are concerned, that Article 141 of the CCP did not allow a compensation claim for damage suffered as a result of procedural deficiencies in proceedings brought to challenge pre-trial detention (see Kocamış and Kurt, cited above, § 39, and the cases cited therein). Having reviewed the parties’ submissions, the Court sees no reason to depart from its findings in the above‑mentioned cases. It therefore concludes that the objection raised by the Government on this account must be dismissed.

189. The Government secondly asserted that the applicants could have brought an action for a full remedy in the administrative courts, seeking compensation for the alleged damage sustained (see paragraph 184 above). The Court observes that the Government have not specified the complaint in relation to which the applicants should have pursued this remedy – that is, whether it would have offered any prospect of success in respect of their complaints under Articles 2 and 3, or those under Article 5, or both. It also observes, however, that the present applications were made when the applicants were still detained in circumstances allegedly incompatible with their rights under Articles 2, 3 and 5 of the Convention, which is decisive in determining the effectiveness of the remedy in question for all the provisions at issue.

190. The Court observes in this connection that where a person is held in conditions allegedly incompatible with the requirements of Article 2 or 3 of the Convention, the States Parties are expected to establish, over and above a compensatory remedy, an effective mechanism in order to put a rapid end to any such treatment (see Ananyev and Others v. Russia, nos. 42525/07 and 60800/08, § 98, 10 January 2012, and İlerde and Others v. Türkiye, nos. 35614/19 and 10 others, § 157, 5 December 2023). The Court similarly observes that a remedy that does not afford a possibility of release cannot be regarded as an effective remedy for the purposes of Article 5 of the Convention while the deprivation of liberty is ongoing (see Selahattin Demirtaş, cited above, § 207).

191. The Government did not argue that the administrative action it suggested had a preventive component as would be required in the present circumstances under both Articles 2 and 3 and Article 5, since it could not have led to the improvement of the conditions of detention or offered a prospect of release. Nor did they point to any decisions where the administrative courts had engaged with complaints similar to those raised by the applicants. In these circumstances, the Court finds no basis to conclude that bringing an administrative action would have provided the applicants with an effective remedy within the meaning of Article 35 § 1 of the Convention, and therefore dismisses the Government’s objection.

192. The Government lastly argued that the applicants had applied to the Court while their individual applications were still pending before the Constitutional Court. The Court acknowledges that compliance with the requirement to exhaust domestic remedies is normally assessed with reference to the date on which the application was lodged with the Court. It nevertheless accepts that the last stage of a particular remedy may be reached after the application has been lodged but before its admissibility has been determined (see Selahattin Demirtaş, cited above, § 193).

193. In the present case, the applicants lodged individual applications with the Constitutional Court on 22 June 2017 (see paragraph 89 above). The Constitutional Court gave its judgment on 15 September 2021 (see paragraphs 98 above), that is, before the Court’s decision on admissibility. The Court therefore also dismisses that objection raised by the Government.

194. Having regard to its findings in paragraphs 182, 188, 191 and 193 above, the Court dismisses the preliminary objections raised by the Government. The question of the admissibility of the applicants’ complaints will, however, be determined separately as part of the examination of the relevant complaints (see paragraphs 212, 257, 312 and 315 below).
V. ALLEGED VIOLATION OF ARTICLES 2 AND 3 OF THE CONVENTION

195. Relying on Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention, the applicants complained that their pre-trial detention had put their lives and physical integrity at risk beyond the dangers inherent in the hunger strike in which they had engaged. On the one hand, the conditions of their detention were manifestly inappropriate to their situation and, on the other hand, they had no access to a doctor of their own choosing that could provide them with adequate medical care. In so far as relevant, Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention read as follows:
“1. Everyone’s right to life shall be protected by law. (...)”
“No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.”
A. The parties’ submissions

196. The applicants emphasised that their complaints did not relate to the risks inherent in hunger striking, which they had knowingly assumed; they rather concerned the exacerbation of those risks by the conditions under which they were compelled to continue their hunger strike following their allegedly arbitrary detention.

197. They argued in this connection that from the very start of their detention, their requests to be examined by doctors of their own choosing had been refused. On the few occasions when they were granted access to their own doctor, doctors from the State hospitals were also present during the consultations, which ultimately led them to refuse further consultations altogether. Moreover, following her transfer from the ICU to the prison ward at the Numune Hospital on 9 October 2017 (see paragraph 60 above), the Ankara Medical Association’s repeated requests to examine the second applicant had been ignored by the authorities.

198. The applicants further submitted that despite the medical report of 28 July 2017 stating that they could no longer live without assistance (see paragraph 126 above), no assistance was provided to them until 15 August 2017, that is until their immediate family members were allowed to accompany them at the Sincan prison hospital (see paragraph 139 above). During that period, public servants acting under the supervision of the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office were assigned to assist them because of the “sensitivity of the situation” (see paragraph 138 above). In the applicants’ opinion, there was no medical or other justification for that measure, which had forced them to have all their needs, including their personal hygiene, met by officials. The measure had also contravened the requirements of section 116 (3) of the Regulation on the management of prisons and the execution of sentences and preventive measures, which authorised a relative to accompany the detainee if assistance was considered medically necessary (see paragraph 160 above).

199. Moreover, the second applicant’s transfer to the ICU on 26 September 2017 (see paragraph 60 above) without any medical reason had resulted in her being left unaccompanied until 9 October 2017. The Government had argued that the second applicant had been unaccompanied in the ICU for reasons of medical necessity (see paragraph 203 in fine below), but neither the Court nor the applicant had received a medical report that suggested such necessity.

200. In addition to not being allowed an accompanying family member, the conditions in which the second applicant was held in the ICU, in particular the lack of appropriate toilet and bathing opportunities, amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment (see the conditions outlined in paragraph 143 above). The situation was exacerbated by the constant gendarmerie supervision and threats (ibid.), which had also caused the second applicant serious psychological suffering. The second applicant emphasised in this regard that the Government had not responded to any of her allegations about the conditions in the ICU, nor had they submitted any photographs from that unit: the information and photographs provided by the Government had been limited to showing the conditions at the Sincan prison hospital (see paragraphs 204 and 205 below).

201. The second applicant further claimed that the conditions of detention on the prison ward of the Numune Hospital, where she was subsequently transferred on 9 October 2017, were similarly incompatible with her state of health and with the requirements of Article 3. She complained in particular that she had no access to natural light, fresh air or ventilation, because the ward was located in the basement of the hospital and was lit 24 hours a day by fluorescent lamps, which significantly disrupted her sleep. In support of her arguments regarding the poor material conditions at the prison ward of the Numune Hospital, she relied on a report issued by the Human Rights Institution of Türkiye (see paragraphs 161-163 above) and pointed out, once again, that the Government had not sent any information or photographs relating to the conditions at the prison ward of the Numune Hospital. She also stated that during her detention on the prison ward, a number of requests were made by the Ankara Medical Association and Turkish Medical Association to visit and examine her, which were all left unanswered.

202. The Government stressed at the outset that the applicants’ medical condition had not resulted from any act or omission on the part of the State authorities; it was rather caused by the hunger strike, which the applicants had initiated of their own free will prior to being placed in pre-trial detention and had continued during the course of their detention. The Government submitted that the Convention did not impose a general duty on member States to release a detainee on health grounds. They nonetheless maintained that the domestic authorities had fully discharged their obligation to protect the applicants’ physical integrity throughout the period of their detention.

203. In this connection, referring mainly to the submissions they had made earlier in response to the applicants’ interim measure request to the Court (see paragraphs 110, 111, 114-119, 122-128, 134-140 above), the Government reiterated that the necessary arrangements were made for the applicants’ monitoring, treatment and care. They provided the daily log of the treatment, services and material offered to the applicants at Sincan prison and in the Sincan prison hospital. The applicants had, however, consistently failed to cooperate with the State authorities, save for when expressly requested by the Court (see paragraphs 113 and 120 above), although they had not asserted that the medical facilities at their disposal were inadequate in any way. The authorities had nevertheless continued to offer the applicants medical examination and assistance, without subjecting them to any form of force feeding or other involuntary treatment, and had regularly informed them about the possible risks and consequences of their hunger strike. The Government explained that the applicants’ transfer from the Sincan prison to various medical facilities – including, in particular, the second applicant’s transfer to the ICU – had been dictated by medical necessity; the second applicant was duly discharged from the ICU when it was no longer medically necessary for her to be there.

204. The Government further submitted that the material conditions in which the applicants had been detained had similarly been suitable to their needs and had satisfied the requirements of the Convention. In support of their arguments, the Government provided photographs of the rooms where the applicants were held at the Sincan prison hospital. The photographs met the description provided by the Government in paragraph 137 above.

205. No photographs or other information was, however, provided regarding the conditions in which the second applicant was held in the ICU and the prison ward of the Numune Hospital from 26 September 2017 onwards, or about her medical supervision during that period. The Government stated only that the second applicant’s needs were met by the health officers and patient caregivers, and that she was provided with herbal teas as requested. The Government did, however, submit records showing that on 8 November 2017 the second applicant was moved to another room on the prison ward, which was still in the basement of the building but received more sunlight. The applicant, however, maintained her complaint that there was insufficient natural light, air and ventilation in her room (see paragraph 201 above).

206. As regards the assistance provided to the applicants to meet their daily needs, the Government reiterated that as of 15 August 2017, they were both accompanied by a family member at the Sincan prison hospital on a 24‑hour basis (see paragraph 139 above). The medical requirements of the ICU meant that no assistance from a family member could be provided to the second applicant during her stay there, but she was accompanied by her sister once again following her transfer from the ICU to the prison ward of the Numune Hospital.

207. As for the applicants’ claims that they were not able to consult with a doctor of their own choice, the Government argued that there had been an opportunity for such consultation on 15 August 2017, which the applicants had rejected, as they demanded a private consultation with their doctors (see paragraph 136 above). The Government argued that the applicants had made no further request to consult doctors of their choice.

208. The Government further contended that the applicants’ state of health had been taken into consideration in the conduct of the criminal proceedings against them and in deciding whether to extend their detention. In this connection, the trial court had routinely sought medical opinion on whether their appearance at the hearings would entail a risk to their health, and on one occasion the panel of judges had even attended the hospital to obtain the second applicant’s statement (see paragraph 75 above). The Government also informed the Court that a medical commission had been set up at the Numune Hospital to supervise the applicants’ situation. This commission decided on whether it was appropriate for the applicants to attend the court hearings and whether the state of their health meant they should no longer be kept in detention. This commission gave the trial court its opinion on the applicants’ health before each hearing.
B. The Court’s assessment

209. The Court notes at the outset that it is unable to ascertain, on the basis of the material before it, whether the applicants raised all their complaints under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention with the Constitutional Court, particularly the complaints relating to their detention in the period following the lodging of their applications with that court on 22 June 2017 (see paragraphs 89-93 and paragraph 173 above).

210. The Court also notes, however, that the Government did not raise a plea of non-exhaustion in this respect, their preliminary objection being limited to the fact that the proceedings in the Constitutional Court were still pending when the present applications were lodged with the Court (see paragraph 185 above). Since the Court cannot rule on the issue of exhaustion of domestic remedies under Article 35 of the Convention of its own motion, it is not prevented from examining the applicants’ complaints which relate to that subsequent period (see International Bank for Commerce and Development AD and Others v. Bulgaria, no. 7031/05, § 131, 2 June 2016, and Aydın Sefa Akay v. Türkiye, no. 59/17, § 95, 23 April 2024).

211. The Court observes in any event that the Constitutional Court did not deal with any of the applicants’ Article 2 and 3 complaints because they had in the meantime been released from detention (see paragraph 102 above), notwithstanding that they were still in detention when they lodged their applications with that court and had remained in detention for a further four months after that.

212. Having regard to the foregoing, and to its findings in paragraph 194 above, the Court considers that the applicants’ complaints under Articles 2 and 3 are neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on any other grounds listed in Article 35 of the Convention. They must therefore be declared admissible.

213. The Court reiterates that the first sentence of Article 2 requires the State not only to refrain from the “intentional” taking of life, but also to take appropriate steps to safeguard the lives of those within its jurisdiction (see, amongst many other authorities, Calvelli and Ciglio v. Italy [GC], no. 32967/96, § 48, ECHR 2002‑I; Fernandes de Oliveira v. Portugal [GC], no. 78103/14, § 104, 31 January 2019; and Nicolae Virgiliu Tănase v. Romania [GC], no. 41720/13, § 134, 25 June 2019). Article 2 of the Convention may be engaged even though the person whose right to life was allegedly breached did not die (Nicolae Virgiliu Tănase, cited above, §§ 139-45). It has moreover held that the obligation to protect the lives of prisoners entails providing them with proper medical care so as to prevent any fatal outcome (see Taïs v. France, no. 39922/03, § 98, 1 June 2006).

214. The Court further reiterates that Article 3 of the Convention, together with Article 2, enshrines one of the most fundamental values of democratic societies, and prohibits torture or inhuman or degrading treatment in absolute terms, irrespective of the circumstances and the victim’s behaviour (see, among other authorities, Bouyid v. Belgium [GC], no. 23380/09, § 81, ECHR 2015 and the cases cited therein, and Rooman v. Belgium [GC], no. 18052/11, § 141, 31 January 2019).

215. In order for treatment to fall within the scope of Article 3 of the Convention, it must attain a minimum level of severity; it is not enough that the treatment has unpleasant aspects (see Guzzardi v. Italy, 6 November 1980, § 107, Series A no. 39, and Ünsal and Timtik (dec.), no. 36331/20, § 35, 8 June 2021). The assessment of this minimum is relative; it depends on all the circumstances of the case, such as the duration of the treatment, its physical and mental effects and, in some cases, the sex, age and state of health of the victim (see, among other authorities, Ireland v. the United Kingdom, 18 January 1978, § 162, Series A no. 25, and Dougoz v. Greece, no. 40907/98, § 44, ECHR 2001‑II). Although the question of whether the purpose of the treatment was to humiliate or debase the victim is a factor to be taken into account, the absence of any such purpose cannot conclusively rule out a finding of violation of Article 3 (see, for example, Peers v. Greece, no. 28524/95, § 74, ECHR 2001‑III).

216. For detention specifically to fall under Article 3 of the Convention, the suffering and humiliation involved must go beyond the inevitable element of suffering and humiliation connected with the deprivation of liberty itself (see Neshkov and Others v. Bulgaria, nos. 36925/10 and 5 others, § 228, 27 January 2015). That said, Article 3 requires the State to ensure that all prisoners are detained in conditions which are compatible with respect for their human dignity, that the manner of their detention does not subject them to distress or hardship of an intensity exceeding the unavoidable level of suffering inherent in such a measure and that, given the practical demands of imprisonment, their health and well-being are adequately secured by, among other things, providing them with the requisite medical assistance (see Rooman, cited above, § 143, with further references). Accordingly, although Article 3 cannot be construed as laying down a general obligation to release detainees on health grounds, the detention of a person who is ill in inappropriate physical and medical conditions may nevertheless amount to treatment contrary to Article 3 (ibid., § 144, and A. and Others v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 3455/05, § 128, ECHR 2009). In determining whether the detention of an ill person is compatible with Article 3 of the Convention, the Court takes into consideration the individual’s health and the effect of the manner of execution of his or her detention on it. It has held that the conditions of detention must under no circumstances arouse in the person deprived of his liberty feelings of fear, anguish and inferiority capable of humiliating and debasing him and possibly breaking his physical and moral resistance (see Rooman, cited above, § 145, with further references).

217. The Court also takes into account the adequacy of the medical assistance and care provided in detention. It reiterates that the mere fact that a detainee has been seen by a doctor and prescribed a certain form of treatment cannot automatically lead to the conclusion that the medical assistance was adequate. The authorities must also ensure that a comprehensive record is kept concerning the detainee’s state of health and his or her treatment while in detention, that diagnosis and care are prompt and accurate, and that where necessitated by the nature of a medical condition supervision is regular and systematic and involves a comprehensive therapeutic strategy aimed at adequately treating the detainee’s health problems or preventing their aggravation, rather than addressing them on a symptomatic basis (see Rooman, cited above, §§ 146 and 147). The medical treatment provided must moreover be at a level comparable to that which the State authorities have committed themselves to provide to the population as a whole (ibid., § 147). Where the treatment cannot be provided in the place of detention, it must be possible to transfer the detainee to hospital or to a specialised unit (ibid., § 148 with further references).
(b) Application of the general principles to the facts of the present case

218. It is undisputed between the parties that the applicants’ “life‑threatening” condition, as well as the further deterioration of their health during the course of their detention, was primarily connected to the hunger strike that they began on 9 March 2017 (see paragraph 13 above), that is, prior to their pre-trial detention. It is similarly undisputed that shortly after their placement in detention, the applicants refused all forms of medical monitoring, treatment and care, save for the intake of certain vitamins and minerals, fluids and sugar (see paragraphs 110 and 134 above).

219. In this respect, the Court has held that if a deterioration in a detainee’s health condition is caused by his or her going on hunger strike and/or refusing to accept treatment, this deterioration cannot then automatically be imputed to the authorities (see Yakovlyev v. Ukraine, no. 42010/18, § 43, 8 December 2022). However, the Court has also found that the authorities may not be totally released from their positive obligations in such difficult situations, “passively contemplating the fasting detainee’s demise” (ibid.). In particular, the prison clinicians and other medical officials in contact with the detainee must ensure that the patient fully understands the medical consequences of their actions and must check, inter alia, that the decision to fast is truly voluntary and does not result from a mental impairment of the detainee or any other outside pressure. No less important is continuing communication between the clinicians and the patient during the strike, when the doctors must carry out a daily check of the validity of the detainee’s wish to abstain from taking food (ibid.).

220. It follows that while events prompted by pressure on the authorities cannot, in themselves, give rise to a violation of the Convention where detainees have voluntarily put their own lives at risk, this is so only where the authorities have properly examined and managed the situation. This is the case in particular where a detainee on hunger strike clearly refuses any intervention, even though his or her state of health would threaten his or her life (see Ünsal and Timtik v. Turkey (dec.), no. 36331/20, § 37, 8 June 2021, and Yakovlyev, cited above, § 44). The Court must therefore determine whether the authorities fulfilled their obligation to properly examine and manage the situation in the present case and whether they took appropriate steps to safeguard the lives and physical integrity of the applicants as required under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention, in conditions that remained compatible with the human dignity, regard being had to the ordinary and reasonable demands of imprisonment.
(α) The adequacy of the medical assistance and care provided to the first applicant in detention

221. The Court refers to the Government’s submissions in paragraph 110 above and notes that from his admission to Sincan prison on 24 May 2017 to 31 May 2017, the first applicant was subjected to regular medical examinations and to monitoring, which included vital observations being taken four times a day. He was also regularly informed of the risks associated with a hunger strike. When he refused to end the strike, he was prescribed a daily intake of the necessary vitamins, minerals, sugar and fluids to preserve his health so far as possible.

222. Even when the first applicant subsequently withdrew his consent to medical examinations (see paragraph 110 above), the authorities continued to monitor him on a daily basis and to provide him with the vitamins and other nutrients he had agreed to take. On a number of occasions the authorities attempted to refer the first applicant to a fully-equipped hospital, both within and outside the prison complex, for examination by specialists and assessment as to the compatibility of his health status with detention in prison conditions, but he also rejected these attempts (see paragraph 110 above). The first applicant was eventually transferred to the Sincan prison hospital (see paragraph 60 above) after the medical examination that he agreed to undergo at the Court’s request revealed that his medical condition required monitoring and treatment in a hospital setting, although it did not warrant the suspension of his pre-trial detention (see paragraph 126 above). During his detention in that hospital, the first applicant continued to refuse to be examined, but was nevertheless closely monitored, as evidenced by the detailed documentation provided by the Government, and measures were taken to prevent his risk of infection (see paragraphs 134, 135 and 137 above). His fitness for detention was also kept under review by the Numune Hospital (see paragraph 126 above for the report submitted by the Numune Hospital to the Ankara 19th Assize Court attesting that the applicants’ health did not preclude their detention).

223. It therefore appears from the available material that the domestic authorities actively took the necessary steps to alleviate any risk to the first applicant’s health by ensuring regular and systematic medical assistance and monitoring consistent with his wishes to remain on hunger strike. Where the primary-level healthcare services provided at the Sincan prison were considered to be insufficient, the applicant was transferred to a fully-equipped hospital, which was also in line with the Turkish Medical Association’s recommendation (see paragraph 107 above).

224. In so far as the first applicant complained that he did not have access to a doctor of his choosing, the Court reiterates that it is essential for a detainee suffering from a serious condition to undergo an adequate assessment of his or her current state of health by a specialist in order to be provided with appropriate treatment (see, for instance, Keenan v. the United Kingdom, no. 27229/95, § 115 and 116, ECHR 2001-III). While the CPT has noted that remand prisoners should in principle be given the opportunity to consult and be treated by their own doctor (see paragraph 169 above; see also the Recommendation of the Committee of Ministers to this effect as referred to in paragraph 166 above), the Court has never recognised an absolute right in this respect. The obligation under the Convention is to provide the detainee with any necessary medical treatment, at a level comparable to that which the State authorities have committed themselves to provide to persons in freedom (see Yunusova and Yunusov v. Azerbaijan, no. 59620/14, § 138, 2 June 2016; Wenner v. Germany, no. 62303/13, § 59, 1 September 2016; and Eldar Hasanov v. Azerbaijan, no. 12058/21, § 95, 10 October 2024). Whether such an obligation would entail allowing a remand prisoner to consult a doctor of their choice must be determined in the light of the specific circumstances of each case.

225. Having regard to the material before it, the Court does not find that the medical care provided to the first applicant at the Sincan prison and subsequently at the prison hospital was deficient or below the standard of health care available to the general population, or that the doctors available to him were underqualified to deal with his situation so as to require the authorities to give him access to independent specialised medical assistance (compare with Sarban v. Moldova, no. 3456/05, § 83 and 90, 4 October 2005; Aleksanyan v. Russia, no. 46468/06, § 155, 22 December 2008; and Wenner, cited above, § 80). Nor did the first applicant claim otherwise. The Court observes in this regard that the prison doctor and the chief physician of the prison hospital and specialists from that hospital all attempted to examine the first applicant regularly (see paragraph 110 above). At the prison hospital, he was also visited daily by a panel of specialists from the Numune Hospital (see paragraph 134 above). In addition, as demonstrated by the second applicant’s situation, transfer to a fully equipped civilian hospital would have been possible had his condition further deteriorated.

226. It appears from the information in the case file that the first applicant’s refusal to be examined by a doctor from the prison healthcare system rather resulted from two other considerations: firstly, as a protest to his allegedly arbitrary detention, and secondly, because the doctors provided within the prison system had allegedly expressed disapproval of his hunger strike and had referred to the possibility of “forced intervention” in case of a medical emergency (see paragraphs 71 and 112 above). As regards, in particular, the second of these reasons, the Court notes that the provision of regular information as to the risks associated with hunger striking or the refusal of certain treatment is a requirement under Article 3 (see the relevant case-law noted in paragraph 219 above). The fact that the first applicant was also informed in this context that there was a prospect of forced intervention, which has a legal basis in domestic law (see paragraph 159 above), does not as such raise an issue under Article 2 or 3, or otherwise run counter a physician’s duty to act ethically. This is particularly so bearing in mind that force-feeding aimed at saving the life of a detainee who consciously refuses to take food cannot in principle be regarded as inhuman and degrading treatment provided that certain conditions are complied with (see Ciorap v. Moldova, no. 12066/02, § 77, 19 June 2007). Nor does the Court see a problem with urging the first applicant to end his hunger strike, which it has also done itself on a number of occasions (see paragraphs 109, 113 and 132 above), so long as there was no undue coercion to achieve that result. The Court would emphasise in this respect that at the time of his transfer from the Sincan prison to the Sincan prison hospital the first applicant was informed in writing that he could indeed continue his hunger strike at the hospital if he so wished (see paragraph 128 above).
