227. The Court further observes that the first applicant was in any event given access to a doctor of his own choosing on several occasions, albeit at the Court’s request and in the company of specialists from State hospitals (see paragraphs 114 and 122 above). The applicant’s doctor, Dr Ş.K.F., did not contest the adequacy of the examination conducted by the doctors from the State hospitals, including from the prison hospital, or the accuracy of their medical findings (see paragraphs 116 and 124 above). Moreover, on 15 August 2017 the first applicant refused an offer of a consultation with a doctor of his choice because his demands to exclude State hospital doctors from the consultation completely were turned down (see paragraph 136 above). There is no record in the case file of the first applicant making any requests after 15 August 2017 for consultations with his doctors.

228. The first applicant also raised a complaint regarding the lack of assistance at the prison hospital between 28 July and 15 August 2017. The Court notes that on 7 August 2017, the panel of doctors from Numune Hospital reported that it would be appropriate for the applicants to be accompanied at the hospital by an immediate family member (see paragraph 139 above). Accordingly, from 15 August 2017 until his release from the hospital on 20 October 2017, the first applicant was always accompanied by a member of his family, in addition to being cared for by the hospital staff, who included qualified nurses. The Court notes the delay in putting this arrangement in place. It observes, however, that the first applicant was not left unattended during that period. On the contrary, he was checked regularly, including by a qualified nurse (see paragraph 135 above), and there is no indication that his personal needs were not met during that time.

229. The Court takes note of the first applicant’s argument that the presence of a relative should have been ensured from the moment of his transfer to the Sincan prison hospital on 28 July 2017 by virtue of section 116 (3) of the Regulation on the management of prisons and the execution of sentences and preventive measures (see paragraph 160 above). It also notes, however, that under that provision, detainees may be accompanied at the hospital by a relative only when that is considered necessary by a doctor; in the present case, that requirement was met only on 7 August 2017. The Numune Hospital Medical Board’s report of 28 July 2017, which prompted the applicants’ transfer to the Sincan prison hospital, had only indicated that the applicants were “no longer able to live without assistance” (see paragraph 126 above), and assistance – previously unavailable at the prison – was indeed provided by the hospital staff in the period between 28 July and 15 August 2017.

230. The Court considers, in the light of the foregoing, that the medical assistance and care provided to the first applicant during his detention was compatible with the requirements of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention and that the necessary measures were taken to assess his fitness for detention. It has not been established that during the course of his detention the first applicant was deprived of the care he could have received had he undertaken a hunger strike while at liberty (see Rappaz v. Switzerland (dec.), no. 73175/10, § 57, 26 March 2013, with further references).
(β) The material conditions of the first applicant’s detention

231. The Court will next examine whether the first applicant’s special needs were sufficiently accommodated during his pre-trial detention and whether the material conditions of detention were compatible with the requirements of his health and respect for human dignity as required under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.

232. The Court notes in this regard that although the first applicant initially appears to have experienced mobility difficulties because of the layout of his detention unit in Sincan prison, the authorities took a range of measures to alleviate the hardships he faced. These included relocating his bed and placing a cupboard nearby, replacing his squat toilet with a sitting toilet, providing him with an air mattress and a wheelchair, and installing access ramps around the unit to facilitate his use of the wheelchair (see paragraph 118 above). The first applicant alleged on one occasion that he had not been permitted to seek assistance from his cellmate in using the wheelchair (see paragraph 118 in fine above); however, it is unclear whether this constituted a consistent practice that prevented him from using the wheelchair and there is no evidence that he raised this issue with the prison authorities or the appropriate domestic courts. While the first applicant may have experienced certain difficulties in moving around his detention unit prior to the rearrangements, he did not substantiate, either domestically or before the Court, their extent or severity, nor did he claim that they impaired his ability to meet his basic needs so as to render his detention contrary to Article 3.

233. As for the conditions of his detention following his transfer to the Sincan prison hospital, the first applicant claimed that the conditions in the prison hospital were less favourable than those at Sincan prison (see paragraph 131 above). He also stated at the second hearing that his hospital room lacked sufficient sunlight and ventilation (see paragraph 65 above). He did not, however, pursue any of these issues in his observations submitted to the Court. In any event, the information and photographs provided by the Government regarding the conditions at Sincan prison hospital, the accuracy of which was not contested by the first applicant, demonstrate that the room where he was held had a large window which let in ample light (see paragraph 137 above). It further appears from the photographs that the room was equipped with adequate and hygienic sanitary facilities appropriate for use by persons with reduced mobility.

234. The Court lastly notes with regret the submissions, made in the context of the interim measure request, regarding the hardships and the adverse treatment that the first applicant claims to have experienced during transfers to and from the prison (see paragraphs 122 and 129 above). There is, however, nothing in the case file to suggest that these matters were raised with the competent domestic authorities (see paragraph 129 above for the requirement to bring the complaint before the public prosecutor’s office). Nor were they raised in the observations submitted to the Court. In these circumstances, the Court is unable to establish either that the first applicant was subjected to any such treatment or that it attained the minimum level of severity required under Article 3.

235. Having regard to the above, the Court considers that the authorities made sufficient efforts to reasonably accommodate the first applicant’s special health needs and ensured that he was detained in material conditions compatible with respect for his human dignity and state of health.

236. In conclusion, the Court accepts that the first applicant’s state of health had made him more vulnerable than the average detainee and that his detention – which was moreover incompatible with Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 (see paragraph 306 below) – may have exacerbated his feelings of distress, anguish and fear. However, on the basis of the arguments and evidence before it and assessing the relevant facts as a whole, the Court does not find the first applicant’s detention incompatible with the requirements of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.
237. There has accordingly been no violation of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention in respect of the first applicant.
(ii) The second applicant
(α) First period of detention at Sincan prison and in the Sincan prison hospital between 24 May 2017 and 26 September 2017

238. The Court considers that its findings about the medical assistance and care received by the first applicant apply also to the second applicant, who was provided with the same assistance at Sincan prison and subsequently in the Sincan prison hospital (see paragraphs 221-230 above). In this connection, the Court notes that the second applicant was kept under close monitoring, despite her refusal of the medical treatment and examinations offered – including when she was offered referral to a Cardiology Policlinic –, and was provided with the vital nutrients necessary to preserve her health (see paragraphs 110, 111, 114-119, 122-128, 134-140 above). There is no indication that the medical assistance offered to her during this period was deficient in any way or was otherwise incompatible with the State’s positive obligations under Articles 2 and 3 to adequately ensure the maintenance of her health while she was in detention.

239. The Court similarly finds no evidence that the material conditions in which the second applicant was detained at Sincan prison or the prison hospital were incompatible with the requirements of Article 2 or 3 of the Convention (see, again, paragraphs 137 and 233 above for the photographs and information about conditions at the prison hospital). The Court takes note of the second applicant’s allegations, recorded in Dr Ş.K.F.’s report of 17 July 2017, that the detention unit in the prison was cold, had insufficient sunlight and had an ant problem, and of her concerns regarding the cleanliness of the tap water (see paragraph 116 above). The Court does not underestimate the distress that such conditions may cause but observes that these complaints were not raised in the application lodged with the Court on 29 June 2017 or in the observations submitted subsequently to it. There is similarly no indication that they were raised with the appropriate domestic courts.

240. The Court accordingly considers that there has been no violation of Article 2 and Article 3 of the Convention in respect of the period during which the second applicant was detained at Sincan prison and in the Sincan prison hospital.
(β) Second period of detention at the Numune Hospital between 26 September 2017 and 1 December 2017
‒ The adequacy of the medical assistance and care provided to the second applicant in detention

241. The Court has no reason to question the medical necessity of the second applicant’s transfer to the ICU of the Numune Hospital (see paragraph 60 above), and subsequently to the prison ward at that hospital. It notes that a failure to transfer a prisoner to a civilian hospital when necessary could potentially lead to adverse findings if the prison hospital could no longer provide appropriate monitoring and care.

242. The Court notes that the Government did not submit a detailed account of the monitoring and care provided to the second applicant at the Numune Hospital similar to that made available in respect of her detention at the Sincan prison hospital (see paragraph 205 above). It nevertheless observes that the second applicant was being held under supervision at a fully‑equipped civilian hospital where the staff included appropriate specialists. Furthermore, a standing commission had been set up at the Numune Hospital to report to the trial court regularly on the compatibility of the applicant’s health with detention (see paragraph 208 above). Reiterating its finding in respect of the first applicant (see paragraph 225 above), the Court holds that it has not been established that during the course of her detention, the second applicant was deprived of the care she could have received had she pursued her hunger strike while at liberty. As indicated by the Numune Hospital in the report submitted to the trial court on 10 October 2017, all necessary examinations, tests and treatment could be carried out, should she consent, in the hospital ward designated for detainees where she was being held at the material time (see paragraph 73 above). Moreover, the second applicant was examined by a doctor from the Ankara Medical Association on 5 October 2017 (see paragraph 146 above).

243. The Court further notes the second applicant’s argument that she faced difficulties in the ICU because she had no assistance from a family member, although she had been allowed that at the prison hospital. According to the information submitted before it, these difficulties arose mainly in preparing and recording her daily intake of drinks, vitamins, sugar and salt (see paragraph 146 above). There is nothing to suggest, however, that the second applicant could not have asked the nurses or other medical staff at the hospital to help her, or that she had ever been refused assistance. The Court moreover observes that full-time assistance by a family member was made available to the second applicant following her transfer to the prison ward at the Numune Hospital on 9 October 2017 (see paragraphs 77 and 206 above).

244. The Court therefore finds, in the light of the information and arguments presented to it, that the respondent State took adequate measures to provide the second applicant with the medical assistance and care appropriate to her state of health as required under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention during her detention at Numune Hospital. There has accordingly been no violation of those provisions in this respect.
‒ The material conditions of the second applicant’s detention

245. Irrespective of the level of medical assistance and care available at the Numune Hospital, the conditions of detention in that facility also had to be compatible with the requirements of Article 3 of the Convention and not place the second applicant’s right to life at risk, in breach of Article 2.

246. The Court notes in the first place the second applicant’s consistent and thorough allegations, both before itself and before the domestic courts, regarding the conditions at the ICU where she was held from 26 September to 9 October 2017, which were not contested by the Government (see paragraphs 66, 76, 143 and 200 for the second applicant’s allegations). The second applicant claimed she had had no access to a toilet; she was forced to meet her toilet needs using a commode chair that was placed next to her bed. The makeshift toilet was initially placed in full view; a portable screen was installed in front of it only after the applicant asked for one, but it was not sufficient to provide her with the privacy required as it did not completely shield her from view (see paragraph 76 above). Moreover, she had no means of taking a shower or changing her clothes.

247. The Court finds these conditions objectionable in a number of respects. It firstly reiterates that access to properly equipped and hygienic sanitary facilities is of paramount importance for maintaining the sense of personal dignity of persons in detention (see Ananyev and Others, cited above, § 156, with further references; see also the relevant standards set by the Committee of Ministers and the CPT in paragraphs 167 and 170 above respectively). As the Court has previously held (ibid.), a truly humane environment is not possible without ready access to proper toilet facilities and opportunities to keep one’s body clean, but these were denied to the second applicant throughout her stay in the ICU. Secondly, hygiene and cleanliness were not only essential to the second applicant’s personal integrity but were necessary to protect her health, given, in particular, her weakened immune system resulting from the hunger strike, which increased her susceptibility to infections. Thirdly, besides being problematic from a hygiene perspective, the placement and exposure of the toilet also deprived the second applicant of privacy. The lack of privacy resulting from the openness of the toilet area must have taken a particularly heavy toll on the second applicant, given that the door to her ICU room remained opened and gendarmerie officers kept watch on a permanent basis (see paragraphs 66, 76 and 143 above).

248. While the Court does not consider that there was a positive intention to humiliate or debase the applicant, it finds that the conditions described above were sufficient to cause distress or hardship of an intensity exceeding the unavoidable level of suffering inherent in detention, and to arouse in her feelings of fear, anguish and inferiority capable of humiliating and debasing her. The lack of adequate sanitary facilities and opportunities to maintain her personal hygiene further endangered her fragile health.

249. The second applicant’s situation was further exacerbated by the fact that she had no opportunity of outdoor access, nor was she allowed to move around in her room. The Court refers in this regard to the second applicant’s allegation, which remained unrefuted by the Government, that the gendarmerie officers had threatened to handcuff her to the bed if she attempted to move around (see paragraphs 143 and 146 above). She was, therefore, left to spend every day in bed without any kind of freedom of movement or access to the open air (see paragraphs 167 and 170 above for the standards established by the Committee of Ministers and the CPT in this regard).

250. The Court notes that the time spent by the second applicant in detention in the above conditions was relatively short, amounting to a total of fourteen days (from 26 September to 9 October 2017). However, while the length of a detention period may be a relevant factor in assessing the gravity of suffering or humiliation caused to a detainee by inadequate conditions, the relative brevity of such a period alone will not automatically exclude the treatment complained of from the scope of Article 3 if all other elements are sufficient to bring it within the scope of that provision (see Karapetyan v. Armenia, no. 22387/05, § 43, 27 October 2009).

251. As for the conditions at the prison ward of the Numune Hospital, where the second applicant was subsequently held between 9 October and 1 December 2017, the Court notes her consistent allegations that she was held in a basement room without access to natural light, fresh air and proper ventilation. The artificial light was also switched on permanently, day and night, which seriously disrupted her sleep and caused her physical and psychological distress (see paragraphs 77 and 201 above).

252. It appears from the case file that the second applicant was kept in two different rooms at the prison ward: in the first room, she had no access to natural light, to the point where she was not even able to differentiate between day and night (see paragraph 77 above); the second room, which was still in the basement, received more natural light (see paragraph 205 above). Despite their undoubted access to sources of evidence and direct requests from the Court, the Government did not provide any photographs or other information from which the Court could assess the conditions in either of the rooms (see the second applicant’s arguments in this respect, summarised in paragraph 201 above). It appears however from the report of the National Human Rights Institution of Türkiye, issued approximately one year prior to the second applicant’s detention at the prison ward, that the ventilation and lighting in all four rooms on the ward were highly inadequate and the patients were unable to benefit from daylight or fresh air (see paragraph 162 above). Moreover, the artificial light illuminating the rooms remained permanently switched on (ibid).

253. The Court therefore accepts as established that the second applicant was denied access to sufficient natural light, fresh air and ventilation during her approximately two-month detention at the prison ward, which is incompatible with the requirements of the Convention (see Neshkov and Others, cited above, § 237; see also the relevant standards set by the Committee of Ministers and the CPT in paragraphs 167 and 170 above). It stresses that unobstructed and sufficient access to natural light and fresh air, together with proper ventilation, was particularly vital in the second applicant’s situation in view of the critical state of her health. The second applicant was, moreover, permanently exposed to artificial light, which necessarily affected her quality of sleep, resulting in both physical and mental fatigue (see, mutatis mutandis, Yasak v. Türkiye [GC], no. 17389/20, § 244, 27 August 2024, and Yakovenko v. Ukraine, no. 15825/06, § 85, 25 October 2007). The Court considers that this prolonged deprivation of adequate conditions for sleep must have constituted a particularly heavy physical and psychological burden for the second applicant, who, by the time of her transfer to the prison ward of the Numune Hospital, was already on the 214th day of her hunger strike.

254. The Court reiterates that while Article 3 cannot be construed as laying down a general obligation to release detainees on health grounds, the detention of a person who is ill in inappropriate physical and medical conditions may nevertheless amount to treatment contrary to Article 3 (see the case-law cited in paragraph 216 above). In the present case, the Court has no grounds on which to find that the authorities failed to provide adequate medical assistance and care to the second applicant at the Numune Hospital (see paragraph 244 above). It considers, however, that certain physical aspects of her detention at that hospital (see paragraphs 245-253 above), taken together, had the effect of humiliating and debasing her and arousing in her feelings of fear and anguish capable of breaking her moral and physical resistance, as well as putting her health at risk. Cumulatively, they amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment that was incompatible with her state of health.

255. There has accordingly been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention in respect of the period during which the second applicant was detained in the ICU and subsequently on the prison ward of the Numune Hospital. Having regard to the fact that this finding encompasses the risk to the second applicant’s health arising from the conditions of her detention at the Numune Hospital (see, in particular, the findings made in paragraphs 247, 248, 253 and 254 above in this respect), the Court considers that there is no need to examine separately whether those same conditions also gave rise to a violation of Article 2 of the Convention (see Tsaava and Others v. Georgia [GC], nos. 13186/20 and 4 others, § 228, 11 December 2025).
VI. ALLEGED VIOLATION OF ARTICLE 5 §§ 1 AND 3 OF THE CONVENTION

256. The applicants complained under Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention that their pre-trial detention had been unjustified, unnecessary and therefore arbitrary, arguing that the detention order had been made in bad faith with an ulterior motive. They claimed that the domestic courts had failed to provide relevant and sufficient grounds to justify their pre-trial detention, and that the reasons given were stereotyped and did not reflect the facts.
The relevant parts of Article 5 of the Convention read as follows:
“1. Everyone has the right to liberty and security of person. No one shall be deprived of his liberty save in the following cases and in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law:

(c) the lawful arrest or detention of a person effected for the purpose of bringing him before the competent legal authority on reasonable suspicion of having committed an offence or when it is reasonably considered necessary to prevent his committing an offence or fleeing after having done so;

3. Everyone arrested or detained in accordance with the provisions of paragraph 1 (c) of this Article ... shall be entitled to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial. Release may be conditioned by guarantees to appear for trial.”

257. The Court has already rejected the preliminary objections raised by the Government in respect of the applicants’ complaints (see paragraph 194 above). It further considers that this part of the application is not manifestly ill‑founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) of the Convention, nor is it inadmissible on any other grounds. It must therefore be declared admissible.
1. The parties’ submissions

258. The applicants argued that although the first investigation concerning them had essentially been based on the same facts and accusations as the second (covering the period from 2 May to 22 May 2017), judicial supervision measures had been found sufficient in the first investigation (see paragraph 23 above). Given that there was no evidence capable of extending the scope of the first investigation and no relevant and sufficient reason to replace the supervision with detention, the applicants maintained that the deprivation of their liberty in the context of the second investigation had been arbitrary and involved an element of “bad faith”. They claimed that the second investigation had been commenced to secure their detention, and that detention had been used as a means of punishment, rather than a legitimate measure. According to the applicants, the real reason for their detention was to stop their protest and end their hunger strike, as opposed to preventing them from absconding or tampering with evidence as alleged. It was evident from the request of the Ankara Security Directorate and the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office for their arrest, as well as from the ensuing pre-trial detention order, that their detention had indeed been sought and ordered because they had persisted with the hunger strike (see paragraphs 32, 38 and 43 above respectively). The force-feeding measures envisaged under section 82 (2) of Law no. 5275 could only be applied to them if they were in detention (see paragraph 159 above).

259. The applicants contended that the domestic courts, being primarily concerned with securing their detention, had failed to consider the possibility of less intrusive measures, despite the clear incompatibility of their health conditions with detention. The judicial decisions ordering and extending their pre-trial detention had been worded in abstract, repetitive and formulaic terms and had no basis in fact. A mere reference in the detention order to “catalogue offences” as referred to in Article 100 § 3 of the CCP (see paragraph 156 above) was not sufficient to justify pre-trial detention. It fell on the courts ordering or extending their detention to substantiate how the grounds for such a measure had materialised in their case, but they had failed to do so.

260. The applicants further asserted that the contention that they would abscond if not detained was completely unfounded. This was borne out by the fact that despite having already been charged with essentially the same offences on the basis of the same type of evidence in the context of the first investigation (see paragraph 23 above), they had duly complied with the judicial supervision measure imposed by the Ankara 2nd Magistrates’ Court on 14 March 2017 and had not attempted to abscond. The courts ordering and extending their detention had moreover failed to take into account the fact that they had a fixed address that was known to the authorities, and that their state of health seriously impeded their movement and made it very unlikely that they would flee. They further submitted that even the nature of their protests – namely a sit-in which they had publicly stated that they would continue until their reinstatement to civil service – demonstrated that they had no intention of fleeing. The applicants also added that their passports had been revoked when they were dismissed from the civil service by the decree-law (see paragraph 10 in fine above), which would prevent them from absconding abroad.

261. The applicants also claimed that there was no evidence of a risk that they would tamper with evidence, as had been alleged. In their view, there was, in any event, no tangible evidence with which they could have interfered. The entire case against them had been built on their protest and on publicly available social media activity, and the courts had not explained how such material could be tampered with.

262. According to the applicants, the entire process had been coordinated between the police and the judiciary to secure their deprivation of liberty outside a regular judicial process and in disregard of the judicial supervision measure already in place. They claimed in this regard that the order for their detention had been pre-determined before it was made by the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court. This, in their view, was evident from the Ankara 19th Assize Court’s preliminary report of 23 May 2017, which was issued in connection with the first investigation (see paragraph 30 above). That report referred to them as being in pre-trial detention, before the detention order had actually been delivered by the magistrates’ court. This premature reference to their pre-trial detention could not, in the applicants’ view, have been a simple clerical error as argued by the Ankara 19th Assize Court (see paragraph 58 above), given that the alleged error related only to them and not to their co‑defendant A.K., who was not in detention. The order for their pre-trial detention had, therefore, been ex facie invalid in the applicants’ view.

263. The applicants further pointed to the fact that the Ankara 19th Assize Court had accepted the first bill of indictment only a few hours before the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court issued the detention order on 23 May 2017 (see paragraph 43 above), which, in their view, had been coordinated for the very purpose of enabling the magistrate to rely on it when making the order for their detention. They moreover claimed that the police appeared to have had prior knowledge of the judicial acts that would be carried out in the first investigation. In support of this allegation, they pointed out that the police request for their arrest (dated 21 May 2017) referred to the criminal proceedings before the Ankara 19th Assize Court and cited the relevant case number, even though the first bill of indictment had not yet been accepted and the proceedings had therefore not yet been formally instituted and assigned a case number at that time (see paragraphs 29, 32 and 68 above).

264. In their observations submitted on 5 December 2017, the applicants also argued, in response to a question put by the Court, that there was no evidence that would justify a “reasonable suspicion” that they had committed the offences of which they were accused. They observed that photographs and posts shared on social media had been taken as evidence justifying “reasonable suspicion”, without any indication as to which specific items suggested a criminal offence or why. They further argued that all their posts and photographs had been peaceful and remained within the bounds of their freedom of expression, and that the silencing of dissenters through terrorism charges was a prevalent practice in Türkiye.

265. The applicants lastly submitted that the courts had also failed to show “special diligence” in the conduct of the proceedings. They argued in this regard that the first hearing was held on 14 September 2017 (see paragraph 61 above), some 115 days after their detention began, despite the absence of any procedural steps in the interim, during which period their health had significantly deteriorated because of the conditions in which they were held.

266. The Government stated as part of their observations under Article 15 of the Convention that “the use of detention as a measure was inevitable in the existing situation in Türkiye”, given the threats to the life of the nation by the attempted military coup and the other terrorist acts that followed (see paragraph 175 above).

267. The order to detain the present applicants was based mainly on the finding that they had “continued their acts in a persistent manner” despite the institution of criminal proceedings against them, and also took into account their social media activity and photographs (see paragraph 43 above). In this connection, the Government pointed to the indictments filed in those proceedings, which included links between the applicants’ continuing actions and the DHKP/C.

268. The detention order had also indicated that, if the applicants were not placed in pre-trial detention, they would impair the proper functioning of justice, given that the offence of membership of an armed terrorist organisation imputed to them was a catalogue offence under Article 100 § 3 (a) of the CCP (see paragraph 156 above), that the evidence against them had not yet been fully collected, and having regard to the applicable penalty. It had therefore concluded that alternative preventive measures would be insufficient (see paragraph 44 above). In addition, the subsequent decisions of the trial court reviewing the applicants’ detention had referred to the need to protect public order and to prevent the commission of a new offence, which constituted justified grounds for pre-trial detention under the Court’s case-law. In the Government’s view, the decision to detain the applicants had therefore been sufficiently reasoned.

269. The Government further claimed that new evidence obtained against the applicants, as well as the developments in their medical condition, were also taken into consideration in deciding whether to extend the applicants’ detention. The trial court had in particular taken note of medical reports establishing that the applicants’ state of health did not result from their detention. The applicants’ detention was moreover reviewed on a regular basis: not only were they able to apply for release, but they could challenge orders for their continued detention.

270. The Government lastly drew the Court’s attention to the relatively short duration of the applicants’ detention, which, when the Government submitted their observations on 2 November 2017, amounted to four months and 20 days for the first applicant, and five months and five days for the second. They further emphasised that the applicants had spent some of their detention periods in hospital conditions.
2. The Court’s assessment

271. It is not in dispute between the parties that the applicants were deprived of their liberty in the context of criminal proceedings against them, pending trial. Such detention constitutes one of the exceptions to the general rule stipulated in Article 5 § 1 that everyone has the right to liberty and is provided for in sub-paragraph (c) of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (see Selahattin Demirtaş, cited above, § 290).

272. For the relevant general principles of its case-law on Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention, the Court refers to S., V. and A. v. Denmark ([GC], nos. 35553/12 and 2 others, §§ 73-77, 22 October 2018), Selahattin Demirtaş (cited above, §§ 311‑21) and Buzadji v. the Republic of Moldova ([GC], no. 23755/07, §§ 84-102, 5 July 2016), respectively.

273. The Court reiterates in particular the requirement under Article 5 that, irrespective of the type of detention involved, any measure depriving the individual of his or her liberty must be compatible with the purpose of that provision, namely to protect the individual from arbitrariness (see S., V. and A. v. Denmark, cited above, § 74).

274. While the Court has not previously formulated a global definition as to what types of conduct by the authorities might constitute “arbitrariness” for the purposes of Article 5, it is clear from the case-law that the notion of arbitrariness varies to a certain extent depending on the type of detention involved (see S., V. and A. v. Denmark, cited above, § 75). One general principle established in the case-law is that detention will be “arbitrary” where, despite complying with the letter of domestic law, there has been an element of bad faith or deception on the part of the authorities (ibid., § 76, with further references).

275. A person may be detained under Article 5 § 1 (c) only in the context of criminal proceedings, for the purpose of bringing her or him before the competent legal authority on “reasonable suspicion” of “having committed an offence” (see Jėčius v. Lithuania, no. 34578/97, § 50, ECHR 2000‑IX). The requirement that a suspicion must be based on reasonable grounds forms an essential part of the safeguard against arbitrary arrest and detention. What is “reasonable” depends on all the circumstances, but the facts which raise a suspicion need not be of the same level as those necessary to justify a conviction, or even the bringing of a charge (see Merabishvili v. Georgia [GC], no. 72508/13, § 184, 28 November 2017).

276. In the specific context of the first limb of sub-paragraph (c) of paragraph 1 (reasonable suspicion of having committed an offence) of Article 5, the Court has further held that “[i]n order for deprivation of liberty to be considered free from arbitrariness, it does not suffice that this measure is executed in conformity with national law; it must also be necessary in the circumstances” (S., V. and A. v. Denmark, cited above, § 77, with further references). The reasoning of the decision ordering detention is, therefore, a relevant factor in determining whether a person’s detention must be considered as arbitrary (see Mooren v. Germany [GC], no. 11364/03, § 79, 9 July 2009).

277. Detention pursuant to Article 5 § 1 (c) must moreover embody a proportionality requirement, which implies a reasoned decision balancing the relevant arguments for and against release (see Ladent v. Poland, no. 11036/03, § 55, ECHR 2008-... (extracts); Taran v. Ukraine, no. 31898/06, § 68, 17 October 2013; and Matchavariani v. Georgia, no. 46852/21, § 60 and 66, 20 May 2025). If other, less severe, measures are sufficient to achieve the aim sought with pre-trial detention, then the deprivation of liberty is not compatible with Article 5 § 1 (c) of the Convention (see Bolech v. Switzerland, no. 30138/12, § 45, 29 October 2013).

278. A similar test is applied by the Court in the related Article 5 § 3 context of pre-trial detention – which forms a whole with Article 5 § 1 (c) and which similarly provides a guarantee against arbitrary or unjustified deprivation of liberty (see Aquilina v. Malta [GC], no. 25642/94, § 47, ECHR 1999-III) – when examining the relevance and sufficiency of the reasons given by the domestic authorities for maintaining pre-trial detention (see S., V. and A. v. Denmark, cited above, § 77, and the cases cited therein, and Ladent, cited above, § 55). The Court reiterates in particular that the requirement on the judicial officer to give relevant and sufficient reasons for the detention – in addition to the persistence of reasonable suspicion – applies already at the time of the first decision ordering detention on remand (see Buzadji, cited above, § 102). Whether it is reasonable for an accused to remain in detention must be assessed on the facts of each case and according to its specific features (see Buzadji, cited above, § 90). Detention can be justified only if there are actual indications of a genuine requirement of public interest which, notwithstanding the presumption of innocence, outweighs the rule of respect for individual liberty laid down in Article 5 of the Convention (ibid.). The presumption is always in favour of release (ibid., § 89). Accordingly, the competent judicial authorities must examine, with respect for the principle of the presumption of innocence, all the facts militating for or against the existence of the above-mentioned requirement of public interest or justifying a departure from the rule of respect for individual liberty laid down in Article 5, and must set them out in their decisions (ibid., § 91).

279. Justifications which have been deemed “relevant” and “sufficient” reasons in the Court’s case-law (in addition to the existence of reasonable suspicion) have included such grounds as the danger of absconding, the risk of pressure being brought to bear on witnesses or of evidence being tampered with, the risk of collusion, the risk of reoffending, the risk of causing public disorder and the need to protect the detainee (ibid., § 88, and Merabishvili, cited above, § 222).

280. The Court has emphasised in its case-law relating to both paragraphs (1) and (3) of Article 5 that the arguments for and against – including the risk that the accused might hinder the proper conduct of the proceedings, might reoffend or disrupt the public order – must be duly substantiated, and the authorities’ reasoning on those points cannot be abstract, general or stereotyped (see Merabishvili, cited above, § 222; Taran, cited above, § 69; Tsvetkova and Others v. Russia, nos. 54381/08 and 5 others, § 120, 10 April 2018; Bluks Savickis v. Latvia, no. 44570/19, § 36, 13 June 2024; and Matchavariani, cited above, § 66). Moreover, when deciding whether a person should be released or detained, the authorities must consider alternative means of ensuring his or her appearance at trial (see Buzadji, cited above, § 87; S.V. and A. v. Denmark, cited above, § 77; and Sanchez i Picanyol and Others v. Spain, nos. 25608/20 and 2 others, § 283, 6 November 2025).
(b) Application of the general principles to the facts of the present case
(i) Period to be taken into consideration

281. The Court notes that the period of detention to be taken into consideration for the purposes of the present examination started when the applicants were arrested on 23 May 2017 (paragraph 35 above) and ended when the first-instance court delivered its judgment on 1 December 2017, acquitting the first applicant and convicting the second applicant (see paragraphs 84-86 above). The Court acknowledges that the first applicant had meanwhile been under house arrest since 20 October 2017 (see paragraph 81 above). It reiterates, however, that house arrest also constitutes “deprivation of liberty” within the meaning of Article 5 (see Buzadji, cited above, § 104, with further references). The requirements of that provision therefore continue to apply, even if house arrest may imply fewer restrictions and a lesser degree of suffering or inconvenience (ibid., §§ 111‑114). The Court notes that the respondent Government have not made any arguments that call for a departure from this principle on the present facts.

282. The same considerations apply to the periods during which the applicants were hospitalised. The Court finds, on the basis of the unrefuted information before it, that the applicants’ transfer to various hospitals did not alter the nature of the preventive measure applied to them, with the result that they remained legally “remand prisoners” within the meaning of domestic law. The authorities therefore remained bound to respect the requirements of Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 during those periods (see, mutatis mutandis, Lavents v. Latvia, no. 58442/00, § 63, 28 November 2002).
(ii) Scope of the examination

283. The Court observes that two criminal investigations were commenced against the applicants on suspicion of their membership of an armed terrorist organisation, in connection with a protest they were conducting against their dismissal from the civil service on the alleged instructions of the DHKP/C. In the first investigation, the Ankara 2nd Magistrates’ Court found on 14 March 2017 that there was a strong suspicion that the applicants had committed the offence they were suspected of but did not consider it necessary to order their pre-trial detention, as it considered that judicial supervision measures would suffice in the circumstances (see paragraph 23 above). This investigation resulted in the filing of an indictment against the applicants on 2 May 2017 on two charges – namely, membership of an armed terrorist organisation (Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code) and disseminating terrorist propaganda (section 7 (2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act) (see paragraph 25 above).

284. A second investigation was subsequently commenced to cover the applicants’ continuing acts of the same nature from 2 May 2017 onwards. In the context of that investigation, the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court similarly found on 23 May 2017 that there was a reasonable suspicion that the applicants had committed the offences of membership of an armed terrorist organisation and of inciting or encouraging the public to participate in unlawful assemblies (section 34 of the Meetings and Demonstrations Act). It based that finding, in particular, on the indictment filed on 2 May 2017 in respect of the same offence and events, and the applicants’ persisting actions since then (see paragraph 43 above). However, unlike the Ankara 2nd Magistrates’ Court, the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court ordered the applicants’ pre-trial detention, considering alternative preventive measures, such as judicial supervision, to be insufficient in the circumstances (see paragraph 44 above).

285. The Court notes from the case file that the material available to the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court at the time of the applicants’ pre-trial detention contained no concrete evidence that they were acting on the instructions of the DHKP/C. There was similarly no evidence to suggest that during their protest the applicants had engaged in any conduct other than expressing their opposition to their dismissal from the civil service. The Court further observes that ultimately the trial court did not find that the applicants had taken part in the protest under the direction of the DHKP/C (see paragraphs 84 and 85 above).

286. However, even assuming that the evidence relied on by the magistrates’ court had been sufficient, at the initial stage of the proceedings, to give rise to a “reasonable suspicion” within the meaning of Article 5 § 1 (c) that they were members of the DHKP/C terrorist organisation (see Selahattin Demirtaş, cited above, § 315 as to the level of factual justification needed at the stage of suspicion), the Court finds that to be insufficient to declare the applicants’ detention compatible with Article 5 § 1 in the circumstances of the present case.

287. The Court notes in this regard that the thrust of the applicants’ complaint under Article 5 § 1 was that their detention, imposed notwithstanding the judicial supervision order already in place in respect of the same offence, had been unjustified, unnecessary and therefore arbitrary. They argued that its purpose had been to put an end to their protest and hunger strike, thereby suppressing dissent, rather than to pursue any of the grounds for detention formally relied on by the domestic courts in their stereotyped reasoning (see the applicants’ arguments, summarised in paragraph 258 above).

288. The Court deems it appropriate, on the specific facts of the present case, to examine the applicants’ complaints in this regard under Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention simultaneously, given the close affinity between the principles developed under those provisions as set out in paragraphs 276‑280 above (for a similar approach, see Korneykova v. Ukraine, no. 39884/05, § 38, 19 January 2012; Sizarev v. Ukraine, no. 17116/04, §§ 161-164, 17 January 2013; Taran, cited above, § 70; Krivolapov v. Ukraine, no. 5406/07, § 99, 2 October 2018; and Cviková v. Slovakia, nos. 615/21 and 2 others, § 71, 13 June 2024).
(iii) Whether the applicants’ pre-trial detention was justified and necessary in keeping with the requirements of Article 5 §§ 1 and 3

289. The Court observes that under Turkish law the assessment of the necessity of placing and keeping a suspect in pre-trial detention is an integral component of the legal assessment of whether there should be a deprivation of liberty (see Articles 100 and 101 of the CCP cited in paragraphs 156 and 157 above; see also Tercan v. Turkey, no. 6158/18, § 172, 29 June 2021). The wording of Article 100 of the CCP allows a person to be placed in pre-trial detention only if there is a strong suspicion that he or she has committed the offence of which he or she is accused and if, in addition, there exists a ground for detention. These two conditions are cumulative: there must be both a strong suspicion and at least one ground establishing the necessity of detention (see Lütfiye Zengin and Others v. Turkey, no. 36443/06, § 83, 14 April 2015, and Agit Demir v. Turkey, no. 36475/10, § 39, 27 February 2018). Moreover, even where those two conditions are met, consideration must be given to whether a less severe measure than deprivation of liberty would serve the purpose (see Agit Demir, cited above, § 39).

290. In its order of 23 May 2017 for the applicants to be detained on suspicion of membership of an armed terrorist organisation and inciting or encouraging the public to participate in unlawful assemblies, the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court relied mainly on the nature of the offences at issue, and in particular on the fact that the former was a “catalogue offence” under Article 100 § 3 of the CCP. Taking this into account, and having regard to the fact that not all the evidence had yet been collected, as well as the risk of interference with the proper administration of justice in the event of release, and the applicable statutory minimum and maximum penalties, the magistrate concluded that alternative preventive measures would be insufficient (see paragraph 44 above). In subsequent decisions extending the applicants’ detention the relevant courts cited the same reasons that the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court had given, in a summary manner. In three of those decisions, the domestic courts also referred to case-law from the Court recognising the protection of public order and the prevention of reoffending as legitimate grounds for detention, and indicated that the applicants would pose a flight risk if released (see paragraph 59 above).

291. The applicants argued that none of those grounds relied on by the domestic courts had been supported by evidence relating to them individually. Rather, those grounds had been a pretext, and the real aim of the detention was apparent from the reasons relied on by the authorities in seeking and securing that measure. The Ankara Security Directorate’s request for arrest had expressly stated that the applicants’ protest could evolve into a “death fast” and that, should it continue and result in their deaths, the situation could be exploited by the DHKP/C for the purposes of propaganda or agitation and could develop into a Gezi-type situation (see paragraph 32 above). This reasoning was subsequently reiterated in the public prosecutor’s request for the applicants’ pre-trial detention and in the second bill of indictment, as well as in the detention order itself (see paragraphs 38, 52 and 43 above, respectively). The applicants thus maintained that the true aim of their detention was to end their protest and hunger strike and to suppress dissent, and that the second investigation had been commenced to achieve that outcome (see paragraph 258 above). They further stressed that no evidence had been adduced of any developments justifying the replacement of the judicial supervision measure – which had been found sufficient in an investigation concerning the same offence and the same facts – with one involving deprivation of liberty.

292. The applicants’ suspicions were further heightened in light of certain developments preceding their detention by the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court, which, in their view, suggested that the detention had been coordinated and pre-determined outside the regular judicial process (see the applicants’ arguments noted in paragraph 262 above).

293. The Court notes in this respect that the applicants’ pre-trial detention was ordered by the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court’ pursuant to Article 100 et. seq. of the CCP (see paragraph 43 above). The detention, therefore, had a basis in domestic law, and it was ordered by the appropriate court. The Court also reiterates, however, that in order for a deprivation of liberty to be considered free from arbitrariness, it is not enough for it to have been ordered by the appropriate court and to have had a formal basis in domestic law; the further requirement of convincingly demonstrating the reasons necessitating detention, as well as the proportionality of such a measure, serves precisely to ensure that it does not involve an abuse of authority (see the case-law quoted in paragraphs 276 and 278 above). The applicants in the present case effectively argued that they were deprived of their liberty for improper reasons, cloaked in the formal procedures of pre-trial detention.

294. It was therefore of paramount importance for the courts to give relevant and sufficient reasons justifying the replacement of the judicial supervision measure in force in respect of the applicants with detention, so as to ensure compliance with domestic law and the Convention and to dispel the applicants’ concerns noted in paragraphs 291 and 292 above that the process had been conducted arbitrarily. The Court finds, however, that the required assessments of necessity and proportionality, balancing the relevant arguments for and against release and explaining why a judicial supervision no longer sufficed in the circumstances, were not undertaken in the present case, whether at the time of the applicants’ initial detention or on subsequent extensions.

295. In so far as the domestic courts relied on the fact that the applicants were charged with a “catalogue offence” – that is, membership of an armed terrorist organisation –, the Court observes that under Article 100 § 3 of the CCP there is a statutory presumption of grounds for detention (risk of absconding, tampering with evidence or putting pressure on witnesses, victims and other persons) in respect of that offence (see paragraph 156 above). The Court also notes, however, that where the law provides for a presumption of the grounds for pre-trial detention, it must nevertheless be convincingly demonstrated that there are concrete facts warranting a departure from the rule of respect for individual liberty on the specific facts of the given case (see Contrada v. Italy, 24 August 1998, §§ 58‑62, Reports 1998-V, and Şık v. Turkey, no. 53413/11, § 62, 8 July 2014). Moreover, under Turkish law, even in the case of a “catalogue” offence, the judicial authorities are required to consider alternative measures to pre-trial detention (see Agit Demir, cited above, § 39). Contrary to this requirement, arising under both domestic law and the Convention, the domestic courts did not discuss in any way why alternative judicial supervision measures would not be sufficient in the present case – despite the applicants’ argument that they had fully complied with the judicial supervision measure imposed in the first investigation.

296. The absence of any discussion in this respect is particularly striking given that the alternative measure ordered two months earlier in the first investigation had similarly concerned the “catalogue offence” of membership of an armed terrorist organisation. A further attempt to detain the applicants for the same offence in the course of the same ongoing protest was moreover denied on 19 March 2017, given the judicial supervision measure in place (see paragraph 24 above). Besides noting the applicants’ persistence in their hunger strike, the competent courts did not engage in any assessment of whether the nature and gravity of the applicants’ conduct had changed in any material way in the meantime so as to affect the assessment of the necessity of detention. The Court notes in this regard the applicants’ lawyers’ submissions, which were not contested by the domestic courts or the Government, that by the time of their pre‑trial detention, and progressively since 25 March 2017, the applicants had been taking part in the protests in front of the human rights monument far less frequently because of their frail health, and the protests continued even when they were not able to attend (see paragraphs 14 and 41 above). Those points were not taken into consideration by the domestic courts.

297. Although the domestic courts referred to the risk of obstruction of the proper administration of justice and to the state of the evidence, they did not set out any specific facts which had not already been identified in the previous two months and which showed that any such risk had emerged. The Court, for its part, notes that the material in the case file discloses no pre‑existing or new circumstances indicating an intention by the applicants to obstruct the criminal proceedings by attempting to put pressure on any witnesses, tampering with evidence or otherwise. It appears from the detention order that besides the persistence of their protest, the only material evidence referred to by the magistrate when ordering the applicants’ detention was content they had posted on social media, which they did not deny having posted. Moreover, the public prosecutor filed the second bill of indictment the very day after the applicants were placed in pre-trial detention, without having needed to obtain any additional evidence (see paragraph 50 above). Consequently, in the absence of further elaboration, the Court is not convinced that a risk of the obstruction of justice or the state of the evidence could justify ordering the applicants’ placement in pre-trial detention (see for a similar finding, Lütfiye Zengin, cited above, § 85). The Court would also emphasise in this regard that, even when the public prosecutor specifically requested the second applicant’s release at the sixth hearing, because all the evidence had been collected and the second applicant did not present a risk of absconding, the trial court did not discuss arguments for and against the second applicant’s release (see paragraph 83 above).

298. The Court further observes that when extending the applicants’ pre-trial detention in its decisions of 30 June, 28 July and 25 August 2017, the trial court relied for the first time on the ground of a “risk of absconding” (see paragraph 59 above), without referring to any concrete facts. The Court sees nothing capable of substantiating the allegation that the applicants might seek to evade justice. In this connection, it was neither alleged nor established that they had no fixed place of residence. There was also no discussion as to why the revocation of the applicants’ passports, which was effected at the time of their dismissal from the civil service (see paragraph 10 above), would not have been sufficient to prevent them from absconding abroad. Nor was there an examination of the realistic prospects of any risk of absconding given their state of health, which significantly reduced their mobility, as well as the nature of their protest, which consisted of a daily sit-in at a designated location. The Court further notes that this ground was not relied on in the initial detention order (see paragraph 44 above), nor was it relied on again after 25 August 2017. In these circumstances, the Court finds that there was nothing concrete to suggest a risk of the applicants absconding.

299. The Court notes that the trial court’s decisions of 30 June, 28 July and 25 August 2017 mentioned in the preceding paragraph also cited the protection of public order and the risk of commission of a further offence as reasons for ordering detention (see paragraphs 59 and 290 above), which the Government have also referred to (see paragraph 268 above). As also acknowledged by the Government (see paragraph 268 above), these grounds were invoked for the first time by the trial court in those decisions, and even then only by way of a general reference to the Court’s case-law, without any actual assessment of whether the applicants’ release would entail a risk to public order or a risk of the commission of a further offence (see paragraph 59 above). There was also no reference to those grounds after 25 August 2017.

300. An assessment in this regard was all the more important given the absence of any evidence calling into question the essentially peaceful nature of the applicants’ actions, which consisted of a sit-in to protest against their allegedly unfair dismissal from the civil service as part of a mass action. The applicants asserted, and the domestic authorities did not contest, that their protest was supported and embraced by a broad segment of society, and that it was an exercise of their Convention rights to freedom of expression (see paragraph 100 above for the Constitutional Court’s approach in this regard; see also paragraphs 37, 40, 41, 42, 46 and 62 above concerning the support received for the applicants’ protest). The Court reiterates in this respect that “protection of public order” is a relevant and sufficient ground for detention only where it is based on facts capable of showing that the defendant’s release would prejudice public order (see Romanova v. Russia, no. 23215/02, § 131, 11 October 2011). The Court also observes that save for the initial pre-trial detention order issued on 23 May 2017 (see paragraphs 43-45 above), the offence of inciting or encouraging the public to participate in unlawful assemblies, which could arguably factor into the assessment as to the need for the protection of public order, was not referred to at all by the domestic courts, including the Constitutional Court (see paragraphs 54, 56, 59, 63, 72, 81 and 83 above; see also paragraph 99 above for the Constitutional Court’s finding that the pre-trial detention order was carried out only in connection with the offence of membership of an armed terrorist organisation); instead, they consistently stated that the applicants were being detained on a strong suspicion of having committed the offence of membership of an armed terrorist organisation.

301. There is also nothing in the relevant decisions to explain why the applicants’ co-defendant A.K. – who had similarly been charged with membership of the DHKP/C and disseminating its propaganda for holding the same sit-in as the applicants (see paragraph 25 above) – remained at liberty if there was such a risk to the public order. It was argued before the domestic courts that this difference arose from the fact that A.K. was not on hunger strike, which reinforced the suspicion that the real aim behind the detention of the applicants was to put an end to their hunger strike (see paragraphs 41, 70 and 91 above).

302. The domestic courts failed moreover to respond to the applicants’ arguments against the deprivation of their liberty based on their state of health. The Court reiterates, as stated in the case-law cited in paragraph 216 above, that there is no general obligation under the Convention to release detainees on health grounds. It also reiterates, however, that detention pursuant to Article 5 § 1 (c) must embody a proportionality requirement, which implies a reasoned decision balancing the arguments for and against release (see the case-law quoted in paragraph 277 above). The Court in no way suggests that the applicants should not have been deprived of their liberty on account of their state of health – for which they undoubtedly bore responsibility –, but that factor should have formed part of the assessment of the arguments for and against release, at least in so far as it affected the likelihood of the materialisation of the risks relied on to justify their detention.

303. When examining the applicants’ individual application, the Constitutional Court likewise confined itself to referring to the severity of the penalty applicable to the offence of membership of a terrorist organisation. It held that that was sufficient to find a risk of absconding and tampering with evidence, without engaging in any individualised analysis in that respect or responding to any of the arguments raised by the applicants (see paragraph 101 above). The Court reiterates that the seriousness of charges or the severity of the potential sentence may, in principle, justify pre‑trial detention in order to prevent further offences or absconding; however, in the present case, those risks remained hypothetical, in the absence of any specific risk assessment, as discussed in paragraphs 296, 298 and 300 above.

304. It is not the task of the Court to assess the strategy chosen by the prosecution authorities in the criminal proceedings conducted against the applicants. Nor is the Court in a position to establish with any certainty that the second investigation was commenced with a view to circumventing the judicial supervision measure in place and enabling the deprivation of their liberty for ulterior motives, as argued by the applicants (see paragraphs 258 and 262 above). The Court nevertheless finds, in the light of the foregoing discussions (see paragraphs 294-303 above) and the particular circumstances of the present case, that the domestic courts failed to fulfil their obligations under both domestic law and the Convention to ensure that the pre-trial detention of the applicants was both necessary and proportionate and so to dispel fears as to its arbitrariness.

305. The Court recognises the challenges faced by the Turkish authorities in the aftermath of the coup attempt, which disclosed the existence of a “public emergency threatening the life of the nation” as argued by the Government (see paragraph 175 above) and as also recognised by the Court (see Yüksel Yalçınkaya, cited above, § 212 and 213). It has not, however, been established that the failures to comply with the requirements of Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 identified in the present case could be justified by the derogation notified by Türkiye, given in particular that Articles 100 and 101 of the CCP, which specifically require the judicial authorities to provide grounds for pre-trial detention and to give legal and factual reasons as to why alternative measures would be insufficient (see paragraphs 156 and 157 above), were not amended during the state of emergency (see, for a similar finding, Tercan, cited above, § 188).

306. There has accordingly been a violation of Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention on the facts of the present case. Given this conclusion, the Court does not consider it necessary to examine the other aspects of the complaints under those provisions (see, for a similar approach, Kolomenskiy v. Russia, no. 27297/07, § 88, 13 December 2016, and Tercan, cited above, § 188; see also, concerning, in general, the Court’s power to confine its examination to the main legal question(s) in an application and to refrain from examining individualised complaints raising issues outside the core issue decided by it, Tsaava, cited above, §§ 228-29).
VII. ALLEGED VIOLATION OF ARTICLE 5 § 4 OF THE CONVENTION

307. The applicants complained under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention that the domestic courts had failed to conduct an effective review of the lawfulness of their detention. They further argued that the restriction of their access to the investigation files in both sets of proceedings had prevented them from effectively challenging the lawfulness of their detention. Article 5 § 4 of the Convention provides as follows:

“Everyone who is deprived of his liberty by arrest or detention shall be entitled to take proceedings by which the lawfulness of his detention shall be decided speedily by a court and his release ordered if the detention is not lawful.”

308. The Government argued that no restriction had been imposed in the investigation related to the applicants’ pre-trial detention, namely the second investigation. The applicants’ lawyers had therefore been able to consult the case file and obtain copies of any documents. The Government contended that in any event, all the charges and the evidence for those charges had been laid out in the indictment of 24 May 2017 (paragraph 50 above) that was filed the day after the order for the applicants’ detention. The applicants were therefore able to challenge their detention, which they had done on a number of occasions. They had never argued that their ability to bring those challenges had been restricted because they could not access certain documents in the investigation file.

309. The applicants contested the Government’s argument that no restriction had been put in place in respect of the second investigation, and submitted a copy of the relevant restriction order (see paragraph 39 above). They claimed that while the restriction had been in place for one day only, it had nevertheless significantly prejudiced their right to object to their pre-trial detention. They claimed in this connection that although their pre-trial detention had been justified, inter alia, by the fact that not all the evidence against them had yet been collected, the public prosecutor was able to file an indictment the very next day. Having been denied access to the investigation file, their lawyers were unable to contest this inconsistency.

310. In so far as the applicants complained of the failure of the domestic courts to conduct an effective review of the lawfulness of their detention, the Court considers that that matter has already been sufficiently dealt with under Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 (see paragraphs 304-306 above) and that no separate issue arises under Article 5 § 4. However, the applicants have also complained about the restriction of their access to the investigation files, which raises a distinct procedural issue under Article 5 § 4.

311. The Court reiterates in this connection the general principles concerning the right of access to an investigation file within the context of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention (see, in particular, Schöps v. Germany, no. 25116/94, § 44, ECHR 2001-I; Mooren, cited above, § 124; and Yüksekdağ Şenoğlu and Others v. Türkiye, nos. 14332/17 and 12 others, §§ 573-77, 8 November 2022).

312. As regards the complaint concerning the restriction order in the first investigation file, the Court notes that the applicants were not placed in pre‑trial detention in the context of that investigation (see paragraph 23 above). Article 5 § 4 is therefore not engaged by that part of the application. This complaint must therefore be rejected as incompatible ratione materiae with the provisions of the Convention pursuant to Article 35 §§ 3 (a) and 4.

313. As for the complaint arising from the restriction of access to the second investigation file, the Court notes from the applicants’ submissions that contrary to the Government’s argument, a restriction was indeed imposed by the Ankara 5th Magistrates’ Court on 23 May 2017 (see paragraph 39 above). The Court also observes, however, that the investigation file remained inaccessible only until the filing of the second indictment on 24 May 2017 (see paragraph 50 above). The applicants and their lawyers were therefore able to consult all the documents and evidence in the file on the day immediately following their pre-trial detention and to challenge their detention on that basis, which they do not deny.

314. There is nothing in the case file to indicate that the applicants objected to the restriction order. Nor does it appear that they raised any specific complaints concerning access to the evidence or the investigation file when challenging their detention. The Court further observes that this issue was taken to the Constitutional Court as a complaint relating to the right to a fair trial, and was dismissed by that court because the criminal proceedings were still pending at the time (see paragraphs 89 and 102 above).

315. In these circumstances, the applicants’ claim that the restriction in question hindered them from effectively challenging their pre-trial detention, as required under Article 5 § 4, has not been shown. Accordingly, this part of the application must be declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded pursuant to Article 35 §§ 3 (a) and 4 of the Convention.
VIII. APPLICATION OF ARTICLE 41 OF THE CONVENTION
316. Article 41 of the Convention provides:

“If the Court finds that there has been a violation of the Convention or the Protocols thereto, and if the internal law of the High Contracting Party concerned allows only partial reparation to be made, the Court shall, if necessary, afford just satisfaction to the injured party.”

317. The applicants claimed a total of 200,000 euros (EUR) in respect of non-pecuniary damage. In particular, each applicant requested EUR 60,000 for the violation of their rights under Articles 2 and 3, and EUR 40,000 for the violation of their rights under Article 5.
318. The Government argued that the applicants’ claim in respect of non-pecuniary damage was excessive and did not correspond to the Court’s caselaw.

319. The Court observes that it has found a violation of Article 3 of the Convention in respect of the second applicant, and a violation of Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 in respect of both applicants. It considers that the circumstances which led it to find these violations are such as to have caused the applicants anxiety and suffering which cannot be compensated for solely by the finding of a violation. Accordingly, having regard to the nature of the violations found in the present case and deciding on an equitable basis, the Court awards the first applicant EUR 12,500 and the second applicant EUR 16,300 in respect of non-pecuniary damage, plus any tax that may be chargeable.

320. The applicants asked to be reimbursed for their legal fees without, however, indicating any specific amount or submitting any documentation showing the expenses incurred. They also claimed 1,000 Turkish liras (equivalent to approximately EUR 215 at the material time) in respect of their “secretarial expenses”, without producing any supporting documents.
321. The Government submitted that the applicants’ claim in respect of costs and expenses was unsubstantiated.

322. According to the Court’s case-law, an applicant is entitled to the reimbursement of costs and expenses only in so far as it has been shown that these were actually and necessarily incurred and are reasonable as to quantum. It reiterates in addition that Rule 60 §§ 2 and 3 of the Rules of Court requires the applicant to submit itemised particulars of all claims, together with any relevant supporting documents, failing which the Court may reject the claims in whole or in part (see Paksas v. Lithuania [GC], no. 34932/04, § 122, ECHR 2011 (extracts)). In the present case, given that the applicants did not produce any documents in support of their claim, and did not specify the amount being requested for legal fees, the Court decides to reject it in its entirety.
FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT, UNANIMOUSLY,
Decides to join the applications;
Declares the complaints under Articles 2 and 3 and Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention admissible and the remainder of the applications inadmissible;
Holds that there has been no violation of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention in respect of the first applicant;
Holds that there has been no violation of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention in respect of the medical assistance and care provided to the second applicant while she was in pre-trial detention;

Holds that there has been no violation of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention in respect of the material conditions in which the second applicant was detained at the Sincan prison and the Sincan prison hospital between 24 May 2017 and 26 September 2017;

Holds that there has been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention in respect of the material conditions in which the second applicant was detained at the intensive care unit and the prison ward of the Numune Hospital between 26 September 2017 and 1 December 2017;

Holds that there is no need to examine whether there has been a violation of Article 2 of the Convention in respect of the material conditions in which the second applicant was detained at the intensive care unit and the prison ward of the Numune Hospital between 26 September 2017 and 1 December 2017;
Holds that there has been a violation of Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention in respect of both applicants;

that the respondent State is to pay, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, the following amounts, to be converted into the currency of the respondent State at the rate applicable at the date of settlement.
EUR 12,500 (twelve thousand and five thousand euros), plus any tax that may be chargeable, to the first applicant in respect of non‑pecuniary damage;
EUR 16,300 (sixteen thousand and three hundred euros), plus any tax that may be chargeable, to the second applicant in respect of non-pecuniary damage;

that from the expiry of the above-mentioned three months until settlement simple interest shall be payable on the above amounts at a rate equal to the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank during the default period plus three percentage points;
Dismisses the remainder of the applicants’ claim for just satisfaction.
